articles.title: The best scar creams and treatments that actually work, according to dermatologists
articles.summary: Which scar treatment is best for you? Dermatologists share top scar creams, gels and treatments that actually work to fade scars on your face and body.
articles.body: Scarring, whether caused by acne, surgery or another wound-inducing experience, is almost as inevitable as it is permanent. If your scars create textural changes to your skin, medical intervention by a dermatologist is your best bet. However, that's not always the case — at-home treatments can help fade some types of scars into the skin, making them less noticeable, according to experts. Below, I rounded up some over-the-counter options to consider, based on expert guidance. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best scar creams and treatments I compiled a list of at-home, dermatologist-recommended products that can prevent wounds from turning into noticeable scars or minimize the appearance of existing scars. Remember: to help treat scars, experts recommend consulting with a dermatologist first. Best serum for acne scars This Topicals serum is a favorite among NBC Selected editors, who tried it on their acne scars and dark spots over the course of two months. Our editors say it noticeably lightened scars with consistent use. The serum has a combinations of tranexamic acid, kojic acid and azelaic acid, which experts say help fade dark spots and brighten the skin. It also has niacinamide to soothe skin and limit excess oil, according to the brand. Keep in mind this serum has a strong sulfur-like smell, in our experience. Best overall scar gel This topical scar gel from Mederma is a favorite among our experts because it can help flatten raised scars and minimize pain. The gel has Cepalin botanical extract, which helps lock in moisture, produce collagen and renew cells to reduce the appearance of scars from acne, burns, injury and surgery, according to the brand. Mederma recommends applying this treatment as soon as your wound closes and continue using it daily for at least eight weeks on new scars and three to six months on existing scars. Best overall scar sheets ScarAway's silicone sheets mimic the natural skin barrier and provide a moist environment, which allows the scar to heal better, according to Dr. Marisa Garshick, a board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology in New York City. “It helps to hydrate the skin, and the adhesive is comfortable and flexible, enabling you to keep the scar covered and protected while you heal,” she says. In addition to protecting newly healed wounds, these patches also work to flatten and soften older, existing scars, which helps reduce their appearance, according to the brand. You can wear one for up to 10 days, and they’re water-resistant so they can withstand exposure to short-term moisture like showering, sweating and light rain, according to Scaraway. Best overall gel for surgical scars You can apply Kelo-Cote's silicone scar gel twice daily to reduce redness and soften raised scars, according to the brand. Dr. Joshua Zeichner, director of cosmetic and clinical research at Mount Sinai Hospital, recommends this gel to his patients after surgical procedures because it dries fully without leaving the skin feeling sticky, he says. The formula is also clear, non-greasy and water-resistant, according to Kelo-Cote. Best SPF scar gel The BioCorneum silicone gel uses patented technology to help soften raised scars and minimize itching, redness and discoloration, says Garshick. It also has SPF 30, so it protects your scars from the sun, which experts say is important to prevent them from looking worse. Best overall scar oil This body oil, another recommendation from Garshick, combines plant extracts like calming chamomile (helps reduce redness) and calendula (has antibacterial effects). It also has vitamin A to help stimulate collagen and vitamin E for hydration, says Garshick. Bio-Oil is also noncomedogenic and great for stretch marks and uneven skin tone, according to the brand. Best liquid scar sheet (2-pack) The Scarguard Repair Liquid is a brush-on silicone sheet that dries quickly to create a protective patch around a newly healed wound, says Garshick. It can be applied twice daily to not only help prevent scars from forming but also shrink old scars, according to the brand. It’s water- and heat-resistant, and it has vitamin E to keep the area hydrated, experts say. Best budget-friendly ointment for scar healing After the initial wound heals, you can massage ointments like Vaseline onto the injury to help soften any scar tissue, says Garshick. The ointment creates a protective barrier and helps keep the area moist to facilitate the healing process and minimize scab formation, she says. The Vaseline Healing Jelly is fragrance-free, noncomedogenic (it won’t clog pores) and has the National Eczema Association Seal of Acceptance, meaning it’s suitable for sensitive skin, according to the brand. How I picked the best scar creams and treatments Remember that over-the-counter treatments won’t do much to flatten raised scars, and most scars are best treated with in-office treatments like microneedling, chemical peels and lasers, experts say. If you want to reduce the appearance of a scar or hyperpigmentation, you may be able to treat it over time with gels, sheets, and oils, depending on how severe and deep the scarring is. Here are some of the best expert-recommended ingredients that can help reduce the appearance of scars and color changes: Silicone: “After the wound closes, silicone gels can help the scar heal the best it can,” says Zeichner. Silicone gels and sheets, which experts say have the best evidence of reducing the appearance of scars, form a seal over the skin to maintain skin hydration and protect it from the environment. Silicone sheets don’t typically flatten thick, raised scars, but they can prevent scar formation after a procedure or traumatic event, says Dr. Amy McMichael, professor of dermatology at Wake Forest University School of Medicine.Retinoids: These are prescription-strength treatments that help reduce hyperpigmentation, skin discoloration and some skin scarring by increasing skin cell turnover and stimulating collagen, experts say. “Tretinoin (topical retin-A) can help in early superficial scarring from acne and stretch marks, but [they are] not helpful for [raised scars like] hypertrophic scars and keloids,” says McMichael. Retinol, which is a weaker type of retinoid, is available over the counter, and it can help improve uneven skin tone and texture.Vitamin C: This is an antioxidant that can help reduce the appearance of redness and mild color changes. However, keep in mind that vitamin C will not treat the thickness of scars.Hydroquinone: This ingredient, typically found in skin lightening creams, can help fade red or brown dark spots caused by hyperpigmentation or color changes. It’s not available over-the-counter, so you’ll need a prescription. Like vitamin C, hydroquinone will not treat the thickness of a scar. What are the different types of scars? Atrophic, hypertrophic and keloid scars are the three main types of scars and they vary significantly in appearance and shape, according to experts. The type of scar and its physical appearance is a direct result of how your body chooses to heal after an injury, and there is no way to predetermine what type of scar will come from a specific injury, says Dr. Michele Farber, a board-certified dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology Group. Atrophic scars Atrophic scars, also known as depressed scars, are indented on the surface of the skin. Usually associated with acne, this type of scar is caused by loss of collagen during the healing process and results in the thinning of the skin, says Dr. Robyn Gmyrek, a board-certified dermatologist at UnionDerm in New York City. These scars can also sometimes appear lighter than the color of your skin if there is not enough collagen production during the wound healing and skin remodeling process, says Garshick. There are three different types of atrophic scars based on their shape, experts say: Icepick scars are narrow, deep scars in the skin that form a hole or V-shape.Boxcar scars are square-shaped depressions with sharply defined edges. Rolling scars have sloping edges. “They are usually a bit wider and give a curved atrophic appearance to the skin,” says Gmyrek. Stretch marks are also a type of atrophic scar caused by the skin stretching or shrinking quickly. These scars are thin and slightly indented, and can appear white, pink, purple or blue in color, according to my experts. Hypertrophic scars Hypertrophic scars appear raised and thickened on the skin. They usually occur when the body produces too much collagen at the site of the wound during the healing process, according to Farber. Keloid scars Like hypertrophic scars, keloid scars are raised and hairless, and are usually pink, red or flesh-toned. However, unlike hypertrophic scars, which are contained within the area where the injury once was, keloid scars grow beyond the borders of the original injury, according to Dr. Zakia Rahman, a board-certified dermatologist, clinical professor of dermatology and director of the Resident Laser and Aesthetic Clinic at Stanford Health Care. “Scars remodel for up to one year after trauma, but keloids, which are scars that grow out the boundaries of the trauma border, can continue to grow for years,” says McMichael. Keloids might also turn darker than your usual skin color when exposed to the sun, experts say. Keloids are also the hardest type of scars to treat. “We can remove them and employ lasers, topical therapies and radiation, but they are very unpredictable and have a high recurrence rate,” says Dr. Mara Weinstein Velez, a board-certified dermatologist and assistant professor with the University of Rochester Medical Center. Are color changes a form of scarring? Residual discoloration or color changes, which usually look like red or brown marks on the skin, are common after an injury, and often discussed interchangeably with scarring. However, they’re not the same: Color changes are easier to treat and will usually go away over time (especially with consistent use of retinoids), but scars are permanent. Scars can also be different colors. Some appear brown due to discoloration, while others appear white when pigment is lost, says Garshick. Some scars may initially show up as pink or red on the skin due to new blood vessels forming, she says. According to experts, there are two main types of color changes: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, which results from the overproduction of melanin after inflammation on the skin.Post-inflammatory erythema, which causes red or pink patches on the skin due to inflammation. “Oftentimes, patients come in thinking they have scars when really they are just areas of hyper or hypopigmentation,” says Weinstein Velez. “Pigmented areas can take months to improve, but they can resolve over time. But when there is a cut in the skin like a surgical scar or a traumatic scar, or any type of injury that leads to a scar, that will be permanent.” How can you treat scars and color changes at home? Once scars develop, they are permanent, but there are some ways to reduce their appearance. Dermatologists told us the best treatments for scarring are only offered in the dermatologist’s office, and they include lasers and microneedling treatments. Depending on the type of injury and extent of the wound, you should first focus on proper wound care to help that top layer of skin heal as quickly as possible, says Rahman. “Keeping that area clean with soap and water and then keeping it covered as much as possible prevents a scab,” she says. You should also always protect scars from the sun. “The last thing you want to do is to develop hyperpigmentation or a burn in the area of new scar tissue,” says Zeichner. Below, I list a few treatments available over-the-counter that can help reduce redness, inflammation and itching associated with scars. Keep in mind that drugstore products won’t significantly flatten scars, but rather they prevent them from forming in the first place or reducing redness, according to McMichael. To actually flatten scars, you’ll need prescription topicals, injections or other invasive ambulatory treatments like liquid nitrogen or lasers, she says. Silicone and hydrocolloids Silicone — either in the form of sheets, creams or gels — is one of the most effective treatments for reducing the appearance of scars and preventing them from forming, experts told us. Silicone works as an occlusive barrier for the scar, which means it creates a seal over the surface of the skin. It helps keep the area hydrated, protects it from the environment and regulates collagen production to minimize the possibility of a scar forming in the first place, according to Garshick. Silicone also calms the skin, which helps reduce the itching that comes with scarring. However, while it may help with redness, silicone is not very effective at treating pigmentation, says McMichael. Silicone sheets are most effective at improving scars because they apply gentle pressure and can alleviate tension and soften the scar, says Garshick. You may also come across hydrocolloid dressings, which are very similar to silicone sheets. Hydrocolloids are patches that you can place on an injured area to help heal the critical top layer of the skin faster, says Rahman. They also reduce movement and stretching around the cut or injury — especially in high-tension areas like the chest or back where you’re more likely to get a bad scar — to help the healing process, she says. Retinoids Experts told us prescription retinoids like tretinoin (known as Retin-A) and tazarotene have been shown to be effective as a long-term topical treatment to reduce the appearance of color changes, acne scars and stretch marks. “Since retinoids work to help boost collagen production, they can help with textural changes and improve the appearance of discoloration,” says Garshick. However, retinoids aren’t very helpful for deeper scars like hypertrophic scars and keloids, according to McMichael. Keep in mind that retinoids can be irritating on the skin, so it’s important to avoid overusing it to prevent redness and sensitivity of the skin, says Garshick. Make sure you’re only using it a few times a week, depending on how your skin tolerates the formula. Retinol, which is available over the counter, can also help reduce the texture of a scar, but it won’t be as effective as stronger prescription retinoids, experts say. Vitamin C Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that can help brighten the skin and improve the appearance of hyperpigmentation and discoloration, says Garshick. This ingredient can be great to help minimize older scars because they tend to be darker brown in color, according to Zeichner. However, keep in mind that vitamin C won’t improve the thickness of scars, says McMichael. Chemical exfoliants If your main concern is slight textural changes or discoloration, chemical exfoliants can help. These include alpha-hydroxy acids (AHAs) like lactic acid and mandelic acid, and beta-hydroxy acids (BHAs) like salicylic acid, which help unclog pores, exfoliate skin and even out skin tone. AHA/BHA peels are great for fixing uneven skin texture and improve mild discoloration on the skin, according to my experts. What are the best in-office scar treatments? There are certain in-office treatments that dermatologists offer that can help reduce the appearance of both raised and depressed scars over time, including laser resurfacing, microneedling and injectable fillers. Most of these treatments cause a controlled tissue injury that helps the body heal itself, says Rahman. Atrophic scar treatments Your dermatologist can treat atrophic scarring with laser resurfacing, which uses light energy to stimulate new collagen and improve the appearance and texture of a scar, says Garshick. Another option is microneedling, which creates small holes in the skin that also help stimulate collagen, she says. You can treat atrophic acne scars with an in-office procedure called subcision, which lifts the scar tissue upward to reduce the depression in the skin. You can also consider filler injections to replace volume if a scar is indented, experts say. Ice pick scars are harder to treat because they’re deeper in the skin. To improve this type of atrophic scar, dermatologists recommend a Chemical Reconstruction of Skin Scars (CROSS) procedure, which uses trichloroacetic acid to help boost collagen production. You’ll need several treatments performed at least one month apart in order to see results, says Gmyrek. Hypertrophic and keloid scar treatments Hypertrophic scars and keloids can be treated with laser resurfacing treatments to remodel the thick scar tissue. This is usually in conjunction with steroid injections, which can help soften and flatten the scar, as well as decrease inflammation and improve redness, says Garshick. Studies also show that injecting a scar with botulinum toxin (commonly known as Botox) provides the same benefits as steroid injections in terms of reducing redness and itching, says Rahman. Hyperpigmentation and discoloration treatments Certain lasers can help reduce those color changes, along with prescriptions that increase cell turnover like retinoids and skin lightening creams like hydroquinone can help fade those red or brown spots, according to experts. Lasers, chemical peels and lightening creams may be helpful in cases of discoloration. In-office chemical peels performed by dermatologists and aestheticians help with skin turnover and can treat pigmentation left behind by scars, says Garshick. Meet our dermatology experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Joshua Zeichner is a board-certified dermatologist, associate professor of dermatology and the director of cosmetic and clinical research at Mount Sinai Hospital. He specializes in cosmeceuticals, skin care and cosmetic dermatology.Dr. Amy McMichael is a board-certified dermatologist and professor of dermatology at Wake Forest University School of Medicine.Dr. Marisa Garshick is a board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology in New York City and an assistant clinical professor of dermatology at NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center.Dr. Robyn Gmyrek is a board-certified dermatologist at UnionDerm in New York City.Dr. Michele Farber is a board-certified dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology Group in Philadelphia. She specializes in skin cancer treatments, as well as general, cosmetic and procedural dermatology.Dr. Zakia Rahman is a board-certified dermatologist, clinical professor of dermatology and director of the Resident Laser and Aesthetic Clinic at Stanford Health Care. She also serves as the assistant chief at the Palo Alto VA Medical Center-Livermore.Dr. Mara Weinstein Velez is a board-certified dermatologist and assistant professor with the University of Rochester Medical Center. Her areas of research include cosmetic dermatology, skin of color, scarring and hair growth. Why trust NBC Selected? I am an updates editor at NBC Selected who has covered a variety of skin care topics, including products for rosacea, keratosis pilaris and cystic acne. For this article, I spoke to seven dermatologists to narrow down the best scar treatments and highlighted their recommendations for the best products to consider. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: MAHA loyalists accuse Trump administration of ‘broken promises’
articles.summary: A scorecard from MAHA activists suggests the Trump administration has broken most of its promises to the movement. The “burn feels especially raw,” one promi...
articles.body:
Some supporters of the "Make America Healthy Again" movement have begun to publicly turn against their leader, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration as a whole as they demand tougher crackdowns on food dyes and pesticides.

A scorecard released Thursday by MAHA activists, including former members of Kennedy's 2024 presidential campaign, claims the Trump administration broke more than 85% of its promises to MAHA on food, agriculture and environmental health. The makers of the scorecard include Dave Murphy, a former fundraiser for Kennedy's campaign, and Charles Eisenstein, Kennedy's former chief speechwriter.

NBC News is first to report on the scorecard , which offers a window into how MAHA views the administration, and Kennedy himself, ahead of the midterm elections. It accuses the Trump administration of doling out favors to the chemical industry, pointing to its decision to approve new pesticides and hire industry lobbyists and executives.

"We're asking the Trump administration to deliver on even the most basic promises they've made to the MAHA movement, and we've seen over and over again not just a lack of interest in doing so, but a blatant slap in the face," said former Kennedy campaign adviser Tiffany Cianci, a MAHA advocate who authored the scorecard.

About 41% of adults in the U.S. say they support MAHA ideals, according to an April poll from KFF , a nonprofit health think tank. Most are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, according to the poll, though alignment with Kennedy or President Donald Trump wasn't a primary reason for supporting the movement.

MAHA coalesced during Kennedy's presidential bid in 2024, then threw its support behind Trump when Kennedy endorsed him. It brought together multiple social movements, including food safety, environmentalism and vaccine skepticism, under the umbrella of taking on big corporations whose products may contribute to chronic diseases.

But many of these advocates have become Kennedy's harshest critics as of late, arguing that their priorities are being ignored by the Trump administration.

Covid vaccine skeptics such as Dr. Mary Talley Bowden have criticized Kennedy and Trump for allowing mRNA vaccines to stay on the market . Food safety advocates say Kennedy hasn't put enough pressure on companies to remove synthetic dyes and other additives from their products. And advocates for reducing pesticide exposure claim Trump undermined their mission by issuing an executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S.

That dissatisfaction has led to infighting between Kennedy loyalists — including those appointed to key government positions — and activists faithful to their original cause.

"What started out as a hairline crack in the coalition is now widened to be a gaping fissure," said Peter Lurie, president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on nutrition and food safety.

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration "has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming."

"After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again," Schuster said in a statement.

Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said Kennedy "remains focused on delivering lasting reforms grounded in science, transparency, and accountability."

"President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are delivering the fundamental change Americans voted for. In just 20 months, this Administration has moved at a historic pace to advance MAHA across the federal government," she said in a statement.

Cianci acknowledged that many of the administration's actions on environmental toxins and food additives have been outside of Kennedy's purview. But his time in the administration has done "obvious harm" to his reputation, she said, noting that Kennedy's career history involved suing the very pharmaceutical and pesticide companies the administration is now working with.

"To see him not speaking out on the issues that are so obviously against everything that was promised is very hard because I believe ethically it's probably working against his own inclinations," Cianci said.

Kelly Ryerson, a well-known MAHA advocate who goes by the moniker "Glyphosate Girl" and helped develop the scorecard, said she doesn't fault Kennedy as much as the rest of Trump's Cabinet because she knows "where his heart lies."

"I know how deep the forces are in terms of corporate influence on regulators, and it's something that he himself has criticized for years," she said. "[But] the actions of the administration have worked really in opposition to everything that we hoped and everything that Trump promised."

Pamela Herd, a professor of social policy at the University of Michigan, said the MAHA movement was always vulnerable to conflict because it consists of unusual bedfellows: liberal moms who feed their kids organic produce, fringe doctors who falsely claim that vaccines cause autism and Trump supporters who want to remove corporate influence from the federal government.

Over time, though, MAHA's main goals have solidified. A March poll from Politico suggests that removing ultra-processed foods from American diets and limiting exposure to PFAS, microplastics and pesticides were key priorities for people who self-identified as part of the movement.

"What the MAHA movement has always been especially interested in is chemicals," Lurie said.

Much of Cianci's scorecard focuses on actions taken by the Environmental Protection Agency and Agriculture Department — agencies Kennedy does not oversee. For instance, it considers the EPA's decisions to weaken mercury emissions standards and roll back drinking water limits for certain PFAS as broken promises.

Several of the promises that were "partially kept," according to the scorecard, come directly from Kennedy-led agencies like the Food and Drug Administration.

For instance, the FDA asked food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and banned two others that were not widely used. It also proposed a requirement for food manufacturers to notify the FDA when they determine that an additive is "generally recognized as safe." The rule would not remove the additives already in food or prevent manufacturers from adding more, however.

Lurie said Kennedy campaigned on fixing these issues, but "never took into account the practical aspects on the ground: What do the regulations actually look like? What authority do these agencies actually have?"

The scorecard does not mention an action Kennedy has touted often: his January overhaul of the federal dietary guidelines , which encourages Americans to eat more protein and cut out ultra-processed foods.

It also does not address Kennedy's vaccination policies. Both Kennedy and Trump have attempted to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children. And Kennedy last year fired the longtime members of a federal vaccine advisory committee, replacing them with vaccine skeptics. (A federal judge temporarily blocked the change, which is still being challenged in court.)

"If you're going to pick one thing that RFK was successful at, it's very much how he has influenced government policy on vaccines," Herd, the University of Michigan professor, said.

Kennedy reassured anti-vaccine activists last month that they have "a strong and steadfast friend at the White House."

But as tensions mount, many MAHA supporters insist the movement does not need a political affiliation. Ryerson said MAHA voters will likely sit out the upcoming midterm elections.

"The disappointments with Obama and Biden are similar to the disappointments with Trump," she said. "The difference with this administration is that we are promised something very, very different in a very real way, so I think that that burn feels especially raw."

articles.title: Presidente palestino adia eleições para setembro de 2027 | G1
articles.standfirst: Decreto prevê eleições legislativas e presidenciais simultâneas em 11 de setembro de 2027, em meio a obstáculos políticos e de segurança nos territórios palestinos; população não elege presidente desde 2005, e o Parlamento não é renovado desde 2006.
articles.summary: Decreto prevê eleições legislativas e presidenciais simultâneas em 11 de setembro de 2027, em meio a obstáculos políticos e de segurança nos territórios palestinos; população não elege presidente desde 2005, e o Parlamento não é renovado desde 2006.
articles.body:
Mahmoud Abbas, presidente da Palestina, em 23 de novembro de 2021 — Foto: Evgeny Biyatov/Reuters

O presidente palestino, Mahmoud Abbas, adiou neste sábado (10) as eleições legislativas previstas para 28 de novembro de 2026 . Segundo a agência palestina Wafa , um decreto presidencial marcou as eleições legislativas e presidenciais para 11 de setembro de 2027.

A votação para o Conselho Legislativo estava programada para o próximo mês, enquanto a eleição presidencial era esperada para o início de 2027. Entretanto, o novo decreto atribui o adiamento a obstáculos impostos por medidas israelenses e à falta de condições políticas, de segurança e logísticas para garantir eleições livres, justas e inclusivas.

" A decisão de adiar as eleições legislativas e marcar uma nova data surge em meio a contínuos ataques militares israelenses, expansão dos assentamentos, violência colonial e repetidas incursões israelenses na Cisjordânia, incluindo Jerusalém Oriental ocupada”, diz o decreto, segundo a Wafa.

O documento também menciona restrições à liberdade de movimento e a retenção de receitas palestinas por Israel, fatores que, segundo o texto, dificultam a preparação e a realização das eleições.

A Reuters informou, com base em fontes palestinas, que lideranças do Fatah e do Hamas concordaram com o adiamento.

Situação em Gaza também dificulta votação

Segundo a Wafa , as condições de segurança e a crise humanitária na Faixa de Gaza também dificultam a organização das eleições. A falta de avanços na reconstrução do território e a ausência de forças internacionais de estabilização foram apontadas entre os fatores que pesaram na decisão.

O ministro das Relações Exteriores de Israel, Gideon Saar, criticou a decisão. Segundo a Al Jazeera , ele acusou a Autoridade Palestina de enganar a comunidade internacional ao preparar o cancelamento do processo eleitoral.

Menos de um mês antes do adiamento, Abbas havia reafirmado o calendário de novembro em um discurso à Assembleia Geral da ONU e assumido compromissos por escrito com os governos da França e da Arábia Saudita.

Palestinos não elegem presidente desde 2005

Os palestinos não realizam eleições gerais há cerca de duas décadas. A última eleição presidencial ocorreu em 2005, quando Abbas foi eleito. A votação legislativa mais recente foi realizada em 2006 e terminou com a vitória do Hamas.

O resultado aprofundou a disputa entre o Hamas e o Fatah, movimento liderado por Abbas. Em 2007, após confrontos entre os grupos, o Hamas assumiu o controle da Faixa de Gaza, enquanto a Autoridade Palestina, dominada pelo Fatah, manteve sua administração em partes da Cisjordânia.

Desde então, a divisão política entre os dois grupos e os sucessivos adiamentos eleitorais dificultaram a renovação das instituições palestinas.

articles.title: Às vésperas da Unicamp e Enem, aulão em Campinas destaca conteúdos mais cobrados e reforça gestão do tempo | G1

articles.summary: Evento neste sábado (10) reuniu centenas de estudantes e apresentou temas mais recorrentes em biologia, matemática, física, redação, história e outras disciplinas.
articles.body:
Estudantes participam de aulão sobre o Enem, neste sábado (10), em Campinas (SP) — Foto: Isabelly Godoy

Centenas de estudantes participaram neste sábado (10) de um aulão aberto no Teatro Oficina do Estudante, em Campinas (SP), com orientações sobre o Enem (Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio).

Professores de diferentes disciplinas reforçaram que a gestão do tempo é um dos principais desafios e apresentaram temas com maior incidência no exame.

O aulão ocorreu às vésperas da 1ª fase do vestibular da Unicamp , que será aplicada no próximo domingo (18) - o g1 faz um tira-dúvidas ao vivo com professores antes do vestibular, nesta quarta-feira (14). Já o Enem será realizado nos dias 8 e 15 de novembro.

⬇️ As aulas foram divididas em três blocos, com 20 minutos para cada disciplina. Clique abaixo em cada disciplina para acompanhar os conteúdos abordados:

📚 Esta reportagem compõe o projeto Vestibulou, uma iniciativa do g1 Campinas para divulgar informações relacionadas aos principais vestibulares e ajudar na preparação dos estudantes.

Abrindo o aulão, a professora Ana Clara de Gouvêa Fernandes apresentou um levantamento sobre os conteúdos mais cobrados no Enem na área de biologia. Ecologia aparece na liderança, com 20,3% das questões, seguida por fisiologia, com 15,2%.

Dentro de ecologia, os temas ligados ao desequilíbrio ambiental respondem por 62,5% das cobranças. Para introduzir a disciplina, a professora trabalhou questões sobre eutrofização e biomagnificação.

Além da revisão dos conceitos, ela chamou a atenção para a estratégia de leitura da prova.

"Viu que tem textão? Lê primeiro a pergunta. O tempo é crucial."

O professor de química, Eduardo Machado, destacou que o gerenciamento do tempo passa também por saber escolher quais questões resolver primeiro.

A professora Mariana Pinezi, de gramática e interpretação de texto, foi outra que destacou a importância de usar o tempo de forma estratégica ao longo da prova.

Segundo ela, a leitura das questões deve seguir quatro etapas:

Identificar o comando do enunciado e transformá-lo em uma pergunta-guia;

Ler as alternativas, compreendendo os distratores para eliminar mais facilmente as opções incorretas.

"Esses textos cansam bastante o candidato. Então, a gente precisa otimizar", orientou.

Abrindo o segundo bloco do aulão, o professor Felipe Mello, de história, apresentou aos alunos a lógica de funcionamento do Enem, explicando conceitos como competências e habilidades.

Segundo ele, as competências representam o objetivo final que o aluno deve alcançar, enquanto as habilidades funcionam como as ferramentas necessárias no percurso .

Além disso, destacou que a prova costuma exigir análise de fontes históricas, compreensão das relações de poder, cidadania, permanências e mudanças ao longo do tempo, além de um olhar interdisciplinar.

Ao final da aula, o docente deixou uma recomendação aos estudantes.

"A gente precisa ter calma e tranquilidade nesse momento. Chegar na tranquilidade, mas também não chegar no oba-oba", disse.

O professor João Victor Soares explicou que as questões de inglês do Enem normalmente estão associadas a um objetivo específico do texto .

Segundo Soares, assuntos relacionados à ciência, saúde e meio ambiente aparecem com frequência na prova.

O professor também destacou que o exame passou a valorizar cada vez mais conhecimentos culturais. "O Enem valoriza se a sua caixinha está cheia."

O professor Bruno Baruffati explicou que filosofia e sociologia exigem habilidades diferentes dos candidatos.

Em filosofia , o foco costuma estar na interpretação de textos e na compreensão de conceitos teóricos . Entre os principais conteúdos apresentados estiveram:

Já em sociologia , o professor destacou que a prova exige a aplicação do raciocínio sociológico em situações concretas, além da interpretação de dados e da capacidade de analisar problemas sociais .

Também responsável pela aula de redação, a professora Mariana Pinezi lembrou que o texto do Enem deve seguir o modelo dissertativo-argumentativo e ter entre sete e 30 linhas .

Segundo ela, o candidato deve reservar cerca de uma hora e meia para essa etapa :

Por fim, reforçou que os estudantes não devem gastar energia tentando adivinhar o tema da redação .

"Pega esse tempo que você rola a tela procurando os possíveis temas, vai estudar estrutura do texto", orientou.

Penúltima disciplina do aulão, física teve foco em eletrodinâmica .

O professor Márcio Miranda usou circuitos elétricos simples para mostrar como o Enem costuma cobrar o tema e destacou a importância de compreender o comportamento da corrente elétrica e da tensão em diferentes associações de resistores.

Durante a aula, ele revisou conceitos como Lei de Ohm, potência elétrica e a diferença entre geradores e receptores. Também explicou o funcionamento dos circuitos em série e em paralelo, tema recorrente na disciplina.

Os principais conceitos apresentados foram:

Responsável por encerrar o aulão, a professora convidada Thaís Guizellini iniciou a apresentação com uma provocação aos estudantes: saber matemática não basta para ter um bom desempenho no Enem .

Segundo ela, o candidato precisa seguir três etapas durante a resolução das questões:

Decidir se vale a pena resolver a questão naquele momento;

Resolver da forma mais eficiente possível.

"Assim como a língua portuguesa é uma linguagem, a matemática é."

A professora orientou os alunos a priorizar os conteúdos mais recorrentes, realizar simulados e analisar cuidadosamente os próprios erros .

"Vocês têm medo de fazer a correção porque têm medo de errar. É melhor errar uma questão na prática do que no dia."

"Sua resolução precisa ser feita, não perfeita", afirmou.

Segundo ela, entender por que uma questão foi errada é parte fundamental do aprendizado e ajuda a evitar a repetição das mesmas falhas no dia da prova.

articles.title: IMAGENS: Procissões do Círio por terra e rio reúnem milhares de fiéis | G1
articles.standfirst: Dia de devoção reúniu romarias pelas ruas de Belém de carro e moto, além de procissão por rio levando imagem peregrina de Nª Sª de Nazaré. Teve ainda Arrastão do Círio e descida da Imagem Original na Basílica.
articles.summary: Romarias percorreram ruas de moto e rio em barcos levando imagem peregrina de Nª Sª de Nazaré. Teve ainda Arrastão do Círio e descida do Glória da imagem original. Veja detalhes.
articles.body:
A manhã e início da tarde deste sábado (10) foram marcadaspor procissões por terra e água em homenagem a Nossa Senhora de Nazaré em Belém .

Três das quatro procissões deste sábado, que fazem parte das 14 procissões oficiais do Círio de Nazaré 2026, ocorreram por ruas da Grande Belém e também pela Baía do Guajará, que banha parte da orla da capital paraense.

Milhares de fiéis participaram do Traslado rodoviário, da Romaria Fluvial e da Moto Romaria, acompanhando a imagem peregrina de Nossa Senhora de Nazaré levada em uma berlinda.

Em paralelo, também ocorreu o Arrastão do Círio, com música e dança na chegada da imagem à Escadinha, local onde terminou a Romaria Fluvial e começou a Moto Romaria, que seguiu acompanhada por milhares de motociclistas até o Colégio Gentil, onde a imagem peregrina fica até o início da Trasladação.

No início da tarde também ocorreu o Descida do Glória, quando a imagem original da padroeira dos paraenses é descida do ponto mais alto da Basílica Santuário. Ela ficará por alguns dias mais próxima dos fiéis.

⏱️ O Círio 2026 de Nazaré, maior procissão mariana do mundo em um único dia , é neste domingo (11). Mas a programação começa neste sábado (10), que além das procissões da manhã, terá à noite a Trasladação, conhecida como procissão das luzes e que será transmitida ao vivo pelo g1 .

Círio de Nazaré 2026: Imagem peregrina foi levada em Romaria Fluviale Moto Romaria por Belém — Foto: Thais Neves, Manoel Campos e Antenor Filho

VEJA ABAIXO IMAGENS E DETALHES DAS HOMENAGENS:

A Romaria Rodoviária foi a primeira do dia, começando às 5h30, da Igreja Matriz de Ananindeua. Escoltada pela Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF), a Imagem peregrina de Nossa Senhora de Nazaré percorreu 24 quilômetros por cerca de três horas até o Distrito de Icoaraci em Belém.

O público estimado era de 700 mil pessoas entre devotos que acompanhavam a santa e moradores que aguardavam a passagem no caminho.

A Romaria Fluvial saiu do distrito de Icoaraci em Belém. A imagem peregrina de Nossa Senhora Nazaré foi colocada em uma embarcação da Marinha que foi acompanhada por dezenas de barcos pela Baía do Guajará até a Escadinha do Cais do Porto, na área mais central de Belém.

Foram 18,5 km (aproximadamente 10 milhas marítimas) por cerca de duas horas e cerca de 50 mil participantes, segundo a estimativa da organização da festividade.

Círio de Nazaré: Nossa Senhora de Nazaré abençoa ribeirinhos em Belém do Pará. — Foto: Manoel Campos/Arquivo Pessoal

Círio de Nazaré: Centenas de barcos acompanham Romaria Fluvial em Belém do Pará. — Foto: Valéria Martins/g1

Em paralelo, enquanto a Romaria Fluvial chegava à Escadinha, o arrastão da Pavulagem homenageava Nossa Senhora de Nazaré com música, dança e muitas cores do Arraial do Pavulagem, caminhando pela Avenida Boulervad Castilho França em direção ao local da saída da Moto Romaria.

Círio de Nazaré: Moto Romaria segue pela av. Presidente Vargas. — Foto: Beatriz Reis/g1

A Moto Romaria reúne milhares de motociclistas. A estimativa era de 50 mil participantes. A procissão é uma das mais ruidosas de todo o Círio, com os sons das buzinas e roncar de motores das motos.

Ela sai da Praça Pedro Teixeira, quando a imagem peregrina é retirada da Embarcação da Marinha e colocada em outra Berlinda de carro, escoltada por motos da PRF. A distância pecorrida é de cerca 2,5 km por cerca de uma hora até o Colégio Gentil Bittencourt.

Nessa escola, a Imagem peregrina fica exposta aos fiéis até o início da noite, quando tem início a Trasladação, procissão das luzes que dura em média cinco horas e faz o trajeto contrário do domingo de Círio.

Círio de Nazaré: Imagem é colocada de volta à berlinda para dar início à Moto Romaria. — Foto: Reprodução / TV Liberal

Um dos momentos marcantes do sábado de Círio de Nazaré é quando a imagem original de Nossa Senhora de Nazaré é descida do Glória, o ponto mais alto do altar da Basílica Santuário, em Belém.

O momento ocorre em paralelo ao final da Moto Romaria, quando a imagem peregrina chega no Colégio Gentil.

Reveja no vídeo abaixo o momento em que a imagem é segurada pelo arcebispo de Belém, Dom Júlio Endi Akamine. A imagem original ficará em um altar mais próximo dos fiíes na Basílica Santuário de Nazaré nos próximos dias.

articles.title: Ataque a tiros nos EUA: 9 mortos na Pensilvânia, incluindo crianças | G1
articles.standfirst: Suspeito de cometer o ataque também morreu. Polícia encontrou duas mulheres mortas em uma rua e outras vítimas dentro de uma casa na Pensilvânia. Motivação ainda é desconhecida.
articles.summary: Ataque a tiros nos EUA deixa nove mortos em Erie, na Pensilvânia, onde a polícia localizou vítimas em uma residência e o suspeito sem vida.
articles.body:
Policiais reunidos em frente a casa onde ataque a tiros deixou nove mortos em Erie, na Pensilvânia, nos Estados Unidos, em 9 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Matt Barnum/WJET via AP

Um ataque a tiros deixou nove mortos , incluindo duas crianças, na sexta-feira (9), na cidade de Erie, no estado da Pensilvânia, nos Estados Unidos. O suspeito de cometer o crime também morreu, segundo a polícia local.

O ataque ocorreu por volta das 17h (horário local), depois que testemunhas relataram ter visto um homem disparando uma arma de fogo em uma rua antes de entrar em uma residência.

Ao chegar ao local, a polícia encontrou duas mulheres mortas do lado de fora do imóvel. Outras vítimas foram localizadas dentro da casa. O suspeito também foi encontrado morto, com um ferimento aparentemente provocado por um disparo contra si mesmo.

Populares se reunem em torno de cordão policial após ataque a tiros em bairro residencial em Erie, na Pensilvânia, nos EUA, em 9 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Matt Barnum/WJET via AP

O chefe da polícia de Erie, Rick Lorah, afirmou que nunca havia presenciado uma tragédia semelhante em mais de 28 anos de carreira. Ele classificou as circunstâncias do ataque como profundamente perturbadoras.

As autoridades ainda investigam a motivação do crime e não divulgaram a identidade das vítimas.

O governador da Pensilvânia, Josh Shapiro, lamentou as mortes neste sábado (10) e afirmou ter oferecido apoio à prefeita de Erie, Daria Devlin.

Em comunicado, a prefeitura informou que a situação estava controlada e que não havia mais ameaça à população.

Viaturas policiais e veículo blindado em condomínio de casas onde ataque a tiros deixou nove mortos em Erie, na Pensilvânia, nos Estados Unidos, em 9 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Matt Barnum/WJET via AP

articles.title: Assustados, moradores passam noite nas ruas após terremotos no Panamá | G1
articles.standfirst: Tremores de magnitude 7,7 e 6,6 atingiram o país na sexta-feira (9), provocando desabamentos e deixando moradores com medo de voltar para casa. Não há registro de mortes.
articles.summary: Tremores de magnitude 7,7 e 6,6 atingiram o país na sexta-feira (9), provocando desabamentos e deixando moradores com medo de voltar para casa. Não há registro de mortes.
articles.body:
Pessoas observam a paisagem do lado de fora de um prédio após um terremoto atingir a Cidade do Panamá, na sexta-feira, 9 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: AP/Alma Solis

Moradores de cidades atingidas pelos fortes terremotos que sacudiram o Panamá na sexta-feira (9) passaram a noite nas ruas, com medo de voltar para casa diante das dezenas de réplicas registradas nas horas seguintes. Neste sábado (10), famílias continuavam abrigadas em tendas improvisadas, enquanto equipes de emergência avaliavam os danos.

Os dois terremotos, de magnitude 7,7 e 6,6, provocaram desabamentos, abriram rachaduras em estradas e levaram à retirada de pessoas de edifícios em diferentes regiões do país . A Universidade do Panamá registrou dezenas de tremores secundários, incluindo abalos de magnitude 5,8, 5,5 e 5,2.

Em La Villa de Los Santos, cidade histórica localizada a cerca de 64 quilômetros do epicentro, casas e uma igreja católica desabaram. Moradores que perderam parte de suas residências aguardavam orientações das autoridades sobre quando poderiam deixar os abrigos improvisados.

Tony Jiménez, de 90 anos, passou a noite sob uma tenda com familiares depois que sua casa desabou parcialmente.

"Em meus 90 anos, nunca vivi nada parecido. Foi intenso, verdadeiramente intenso", contou à Associated Press.

O terremoto principal teve epicentro a cerca de 10 quilômetros da comunidade de Pitaloza Arriba, na província de Herrera, segundo o Serviço Geológico dos Estados Unidos (USGS). O abalo ocorreu a aproximadamente 10 quilômetros de profundidade e foi sentido até na Colômbia.

Veículos esmagados sob um hotel que desabou após um terremoto atingir Penonome — Foto: AP/Aris Mariota

Igrejas, hotéis e estradas sofreram danos

Os estragos se concentraram nas províncias de Veraguas, Herrera e Los Santos, segundo o Serviço Nacional de Proteção Civil do Panamá.

Em Penonomé, a cerca de 150 quilômetros da Cidade do Panamá, parte da catedral localizada na praça principal desabou. Também foram registrados danos no prédio do governo provincial e no hotel Dos Continentes.

Na cidade de La Villa de Los Santos, a igreja de San Atanasio, reconhecida como Patrimônio Histórico Nacional desde 1938, também desabou. Em outras localidades, grandes rachaduras comprometeram estradas.

Apesar da força dos terremotos, as autoridades não registraram mortes.

O Aeroporto Internacional de Tocumen, na capital panamenha, suspendeu temporariamente suas operações após o primeiro terremoto, mas retomou os serviços ainda na sexta-feira.

Já o Canal do Panamá continuou funcionando normalmente. A administração informou que equipes técnicas realizam inspeções para identificar possíveis danos às instalações.

Prédio parcialmente desabado permanece de pé após um terremoto atingir Penonome — Foto: AP/Aris Mariota

O Panamá está localizado em uma região de intensa atividade sísmica, próxima ao chamado Círculo de Fogo do Pacífico, uma faixa de aproximadamente 40 mil quilômetros que concentra a maior parte dos terremotos registrados no planeta.

A movimentação de placas tectônicas, entre elas as de Cocos, Nazca e Caribe, provoca o acúmulo e a liberação de energia na crosta terrestre, dando origem aos terremotos.

O último grande terremoto a causar danos generalizados no Panamá ocorreu em 1991. Na ocasião, um abalo de magnitude 7,4, com epicentro na Costa Rica, matou 23 pessoas, deixou 559 feridas e milhares de desabrigados na região fronteiriça de Bocas del Toro.

articles.title: Idoso fica ferido após atropelamento e moradores cobram lombadas e sinalização em Campinas | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente ocorreu na Rua Lux Aeterna, no Jardim dos Oliveiras, neste sábado (10). Emdec informou que fará vistoria para avaliar reforço na segurança viária do local.
articles.summary: Acidente ocorreu na Rua Lux Aeterna, no Jardim dos Oliveiras, neste sábado (10). Emdec informou que fará vistoria para avaliar reforço na segurança viária do local.
articles.body:
Um idoso de 80 anos ficou ferido após ser atropelado por um carro ao tentar atravessar uma via no bairro Jardim dos Oliveiras, em Campinas (SP), no início da tarde deste sábado (10). Por conta do acidente, moradores cobram melhorias na sinalização e a instalação de redutores de velocidade.

O atropelamento ocorreu por volta das 12h20, na Rua Lux Aeterna. A vítima foi socorrida por uma equipe do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) e levada para a Unidade de Pronto Atendimento (UPA) Carlos Lourenço.

Segundo um morador, os acidentes de trânsito são frequentes na via e exigem a colocação de lombadas para forçar os motoristas a reduzirem a velocidade.

"Precisa de lombada. Não tem uma sinalização, nada na avenida. Tem supermercado novo, prédio de alto padrão, e o pessoal está abandonado", afirmou um morador.

O filho da vítima também criticou a falta de intervenções no local.

"Semana retrasada bateram no meu carro. Eu peço lombada, peço radar, ninguém faz nada. Hoje meu pai é vítima de mais um acidente. Fazem prédio, fazem tudo aqui e ninguém vem cuidar", disse.

Idoso ficou ferido ao ser atropelado tentando atravessar uma rua no Jardim dos Oliveiras, em Campinas (SP), neste sábado (10) — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

Em nota, a Empresa Municipal de Desenvolvimento de Campinas (Emdec) informou que fará uma vistoria no local na próxima semana.

Segundo a empresa, o objetivo é avaliar as condições atuais da sinalização de solo e das placas, além de estudar possíveis medidas para ampliar a segurança viária, o que inclui a viabilidade de instalar as lombadas.

A Emdec reforçou, no entanto, que é papel de cada condutor respeitar o limite de velocidade permitido na via.

"Somente neste ano, o excesso de velocidade já causou quatro mortes em vias urbanas. Em 2025, foram 53 mortes por esse fator de risco, em vias urbanas e rodovias", destacou.

articles.title: Projeto transforma ancestralidade e referências periféricas em coleção | G1
articles.standfirst: Mostra que vai apresentar as peças será realizada a partir das 13h deste sábado (10), em Votorantim (SP). Programação conta com roda de conversa com representantes dos povos Baniwa, Baré e Dessana.
articles.summary: Uma coleção de roupas criada dentro do Assentamento Rosa Luxemburgo, em Votorantim (SP), busca transformar referências da ancestralidade indígena em moda.
articles.body:
Uma coleção de roupas criada dentro do Assentamento Rosa Luxemburgo, em Votorantim (SP), busca transformar referências da ancestralidade indígena e negra, da cultura periférica e da história da região em peças de moda. O resultado é apresentado ao público neste sábado (10), durante a Mostra Cultural do Terra.

O projeto “Terra Rasgada – Moda Ancestral” foi idealizado pela designer de moda e produtora cultural Isabela Couto Espíndola e desenvolvido em parceria com moradores da comunidade e o coletivo Bando Maré de Março, ligado à Escola de Capoeira Angola e Samba de Roda.

A iniciativa foi construída no próprio território e envolveu oficinas de corte e costura, tingimento natural e expressão corporal. As roupas foram confeccionadas por costureiras que vivem no assentamento e trabalham no ateliê Rosas e Retalhos.

A coleção, chamada “Rio que esquece a nascente, seca”, propõe uma leitura contemporânea sobre a história do território antes, durante e depois da colonização.

‘Nossa ancestralidade não começa nos tropeiros’

Projeto de Votorantim transforma ancestralidade e referências periféricas em coleção de moda — Foto: Divulgação

Ao g1 , Isabela Espíndola revelou que a ideia do projeto surgiu durante encontros semanais na escola de capoeira. Ela conta que os professores, que já atuavam com cultura, apresentaram a possibilidade de participar de um edital do Programa de Ação Cultural (ProAC).

A escolha pelo assentamento ocorreu também pela relação que a designer já tinha com o local. “Ele [o projeto] foi pensado dentro desse território, porque lá é o lugar onde a escola está e onde frequento também. Além disso, acredito que primeiro olhamos para os territórios que estão ao nosso redor”, explica.

Para construir a coleção, o projeto buscou referências relacionadas aos povos indígenas que, segundo Isabela, já faziam parte da história da região antes da formação das cidades.

“Nossa ancestralidade não começa nos tropeiros. Ela é muito mais antiga. Antes deles, este território já era ocupado por povos indígenas, que construíram suas próprias histórias, culturas e relações com o território e com o Rio Sorocaba ”, afirma.

Projeto de Votorantim transforma ancestralidade e referências periféricas em coleção de moda — Foto: Reprodução/Kayan Viana

A coleção foi dividida em três momentos para o desfile: pré-colonização, colonização e pós-colonização. Elementos relacionados a esses períodos aparecem nas peças e também na composição dos looks.

As miçangas utilizadas nas roupas fazem referência, segundo a idealizadora, à tradição indígena de criação de adornos corporais. A trama das peças remete às redes de pesca e ao Rio Sorocaba, enquanto os cortes amplos representam o movimento da água.

Os desenhos presentes nas roupas também dialogam com símbolos de religiões de matriz africana. Para Isabela, a proposta não era apenas utilizar referências ancestrais como estética.

Por isso, o projeto também buscou contato com pessoas ligadas a essas tradições, incluindo o Centro de Convivência Indígena (CCI) da UFSCar Sorocaba. “Para não reduzirmos apenas à estética, é necessário incluir pessoas que carregam essa ancestralidade”, afirma.

Projeto de Votorantim transforma ancestralidade e referências periféricas em coleção de moda — Foto: Reprodução/Nathalia Muratt

A comunidade participou de diferentes etapas do projeto. Os moradores estiveram nas oficinas de corte e costura e de tingimento natural e, posteriormente, participaram de uma atividade de expressão corporal voltada para a preparação do desfile.

As próprias costureiras do assentamento ficaram responsáveis pela confecção das peças. Além da produção das roupas, moradores também estarão entre os modelos do desfile e participarão da feira de economia criativa que será realizada durante a mostra.

Para idealizadora, a iniciativa também representa uma possibilidade de geração de renda dentro da comunidade. “O Terra Rasgada gerou alguns impactos para a comunidade, remunerando as costureiras de forma justa, os modelos que são moradores do assentamento e também a feira de economia criativa, que é composta majoritariamente pelos moradores da comunidade”, diz.

O projeto foi selecionado pelo ProAC Editais, da Secretaria da Cultura, Economia e Indústria Criativas do Estado de São Paulo. A proposta “Terra Rasgada Moda Ancestral” aparece entre os projetos selecionados na modalidade de Design de Moda.

O reaproveitamento de materiais também fez parte da produção da coleção. O algodão cru foi utilizado como base das roupas, os retalhos maiores que sobraram foram aproveitados na produção de itens como decoração, cadernos e bandeiras. Já os pedaços menores foram destinados à compostagem.

A proposta também incluiu atividades de capacitação. Em junho, o projeto promoveu uma oficina gratuita de costura e reparos no próprio Assentamento Rosa Luxemburgo, com foco em técnicas que pudessem ampliar a autonomia e as possibilidades de geração de renda dos participantes.

‘Um território urbano, porém interiorano’

Para Isabela, o próprio assentamento também é uma das principais referências para a identidade visual da coleção.

“O assentamento é uma periferia, um lugar cheio de cultura e com uma estética única que é só de lá, um território urbano, porém interiorano e cheio de talentos.”

A relação com o território também aparece no próprio nome do projeto. “Terra Rasgada” faz referência à expressão associada ao desenho do Rio Sorocaba e à origem do nome da cidade de Sorocaba. A proposta é aproximar essa memória de uma estética contemporânea, combinando elementos considerados ancestrais com referências urbanas e futuristas.

“Imaginar o futuro a partir dos saberes ancestrais é reconhecer que o que veio antes ainda pode orientar o que está por vir. É valorizar conhecimentos, modos de viver e de criar que foram transmitidos entre gerações para construir um futuro mais consciente, conectado à nossa história e ao nosso território”, afirma Isabela.

Isabela Couto Espíndola, designer de moda e produtora cultural — Foto: Reprodução/Filipe Lea Plaza

Além do desfile da coleção, a Mostra Cultural do Terra terá feira de artesanato, apresentação de capoeira, roda de conversa sobre território e identidade, shows de Gabrelú e Maria Preta, e também discotecagem.

A programação terá uma roda de conversa com representantes dos povos Baniwa, Baré e Dessana. A mostra começa às 13h deste sábado (10), no Assentamento Rosa Luxemburgo, localizado na Avenida Vitalino Pagliato, nº 1000, em Votorantim.

A entrada é gratuita, mas é necessário retirar ingresso antecipadamente. Os organizadores também recebem doações voluntárias de 1 kg de alimento não perecível.

O evento conta com recursos de acessibilidade, como intérprete de Libras, banheiros acessíveis e um espaço sensorial, onde o público poderá tocar nos tecidos e perceber as texturas e os aromas das peças.

articles.title: Rio Machado: Corpo de jovem desaparecido em pescaria é encontrado | G1
articles.standfirst: Marcos André Ferreira Santos desapareceu na tarde de quinta-feira (8), após cair de um barco durante uma pescaria. O corpo foi encontrado na manhã deste sábado (10), após três dias de buscas.
articles.summary: O corpo de Marcos André Ferreira Santos foi localizado pelos bombeiros neste sábado (10) após três dias de buscas intensas no Rio Machado, em Ji-Paraná.
articles.body:
Marcos André Ferreira Santos, de 20 anos — Foto: Reprodução/redes sociais

O corpo do jovem Marcos André Ferreira Santos, de 20 anos, foi encontrado por volta das 7h deste sábado (10), após três dias de buscas no Rio Machado, em Ji-Paraná (RO). Ele estava desaparecido desde a tarde de quinta-feira (8), quando caiu de um barco durante uma pescaria.

Segundo o registro da ocorrência, Marcos pescava com colegas de trabalho na localidade de Nova Vida, a cerca de 30 km abaixo da ponte sobre o rio. Após a queda, as pessoas que estavam com ele tentaram resgatá-lo, mas não conseguiram retirá-lo da água antes que ele afundasse.

Equipes de mergulhadores do Corpo de Bombeiros Militar de Rondônia (CBMRO) realizaram buscas na região desde quinta-feira, com apoio de uma embarcação dos amigos da vítima.

As buscas foram feitas com mergulhos em áreas de até 15 metros de profundidade e varreduras na superfície do rio.

articles.title: California high-speed rail consultants billed taxpayers for late-night rides
articles.summary: CBS California Investigates obtained receipts behind the watchdog's findings of wasteful spending, revealing previously undisclosed connections to the high-s...
articles.body:
Well after dark one night last September, a highly paid consultant for the California High-Speed Rail Authority expensed a Lyft ride that pulled up outside the agency CEO's home in Folsom, California.

Just before midnight, another highly paid consultant expensed a Lyft ride from the same house back to his Sacramento hotel.

The first was Denver attorney Brent Butzin, who CBS California has independently confirmed is the legal-services consultant referenced in the High-Speed Rail inspector general's recent investigation . The second was Thierry Prate, a managing director at KPMG, the financial adviser examined in the same report.

Both submitted the rides as expenses associated with California's multibillion-dollar high-speed rail project.

And it wasn't the only late-night ride from the High-Speed Rail CEO's home.

Why were taxpayers billed for late-night rides from the CEO's home?

After California's independent High-Speed Rail inspector general found widespread failures in consultant travel oversight, whistleblowers provided CBS California Investigates with some of the underlying expense records.

We reviewed nearly 6,000 pages of invoices and expense claims that KPMG and the law firm Nossaman submitted to the authority for work from September 2024 through January 2026.

Among the receipts from two consultants, Prate and Butzin, we found a dozen rides to or from the small residential street in Folsom where High-Speed Rail CEO Ian Choudri owns a home.

Another dozen rides went to or from nearby Folsom restaurants and bars.

Many rides involved late-night or early-morning pickups, including two after 1 a.m.

The receipts don't establish who attended the gatherings, what business took place, or whether Choudri was present. His wife also works for KPMG.

But the receipts reveal previously undisclosed connections between consultants' travel expenses and the CEO's private residence.

And they raise questions about who authorized those rides.

What state business justified trips to and from the CEO's private residence and nearby restaurants, sometimes after midnight?

And what influence do these highly paid consultants have over the decisions driving the project's costs and schedule?

The questions come as California's high-speed rail project continues to spend billions, nearly two decades after voters approved a bullet train connecting San Francisco and Los Angeles.

Meanwhile, the authority said it is paying just four consulting contractors more than a quarter of a billion dollars over two fiscal years.

Sources inside the High-Speed Rail Authority say the inspector general's findings point to something much bigger than questionable travel expenses.

Who holds influence over this multibillion-dollar public project? Who makes the decisions? And who's accountable when those decisions cost taxpayers money?

CEO declines to answer questions about late-night rides

CBS California published its investigation hours before Friday's special board meeting to discuss the Inspector General's investigation. After the meeting, investigative correspondent Julie Watts asked High-Speed Rail CEO Ian Choudri about the late-night rides from his home.

Choudri walked away without answering. The authority's head of communications told CBS California that Choudri would not answer questions and directed reporters to email questions to his office.

CBS California had previously submitted detailed written questions to his office asking about the expense records. The authority provided a general response outlining changes to travel oversight but did not directly answer questions about the rides.

In an email, the High-Speed Rail Authority said it is tightening travel oversight, updating reimbursement rules and requiring new training for consultants and contract managers before approving additional travel expenses.

"Only travel that is pre-approved, within contract scope and consistent with state regulations will be eligible for reimbursement," the Authority said.

In a response to CBS California, KPMG said it is reviewing the travel expenses and will reimburse the Authority as appropriate.

"KPMG takes seriously its obligations regarding the accurate submission of expenses and KPMG professionals are expected to be responsible stewards of client and firm resources, said Russ Grote, Managing Director of Corporate Affairs.

CBS California also sent detailed questions to High-Speed Rail CEO Ian Choudri, Denver attorney Brent Butzin and KPMG managing director Thierry Prate.

None of the three responded to requests for comment.

Although board members had reviewed the investigation, none publicly pressed Choudri about the late-night rides or the IG's report during the meeting.

When Watts asked the board chair why he hadn't questioned Choudri about the findings, he did not directly answer. But when asked whether the CEO should speak with California reporters representing taxpayers, the chair said, "Yes," adding, "I believe in communication."

The CEO wouldn't answer our questions. The board didn't ask them.

The receipts reveal why those questions matter, and one internal email connects a late-night ride directly to work with Choudri.

When the High-Speed Rail Authority questioned KPMG, the firm described one of Prate's rides to the CEO's residence as "related to work with Ian."

On that evening, Prate's Lyft arrived at the Folsom home shortly after 7:30 p.m. His next documented ride departed the same address after 1 a.m.

A late-night business meeting isn't necessarily inappropriate. Neither is visiting an executive's home.

But the records don't explain what specific work required repeated rides to the CEO's residence, who was there or how the authority determined the transportation was an appropriate business expense.

Those details matter because California's travel rules require more than a receipt. They require a legitimate business purpose.

And the inspector general found that the High-Speed Rail Authority repeatedly failed to document whether consultant travel met that standard.

A pizza delivery. Another late-night ride.

Prate's receipts also document a food delivery to the same residence.

One January evening, shortly after 9:30 p.m., an Uber Eats driver delivered a $94.39 order from a Folsom pizza restaurant to Choudri's home, charged to Prate's KPMG corporate card

The High-Speed Rail Authority disputed the food delivery, and records show the consultant accepted the dispute. Taxpayers ultimately didn't pay for the pizza. They did pay for Prate's ride home.

The receipts also don't identify who ate the food or who was at the house. But they reinforce the central question about the travel expenses.

What state business justifies repeatedly charging the project for transportation to and from the CEO's private home?

The paperwork says Sacramento. The receipts show Folsom.

The CEO's home wasn't the only Folsom destination.

Other travel records show consultants frequently taking rides between their Sacramento hotels and restaurants and bars near the CEO's home, roughly 30 minutes away.

All of the destinations were in the same shopping center as the Land Ocean Steak House that the CEO frequents, according to multiple sources.

Some rides back to Sacramento began after midnight.

Butzin's expense paperwork reveals another apparent discrepancy.

Five travel forms described the purpose of his trips as "Meetings at CHSRA in Sacramento." But attached receipts document travel to restaurants and other locations in Folsom.

The forms didn't identify those destinations. Their business-entertainment sections were blank.

None of that establishes that the restaurant visits were personal, or that every expense required a separate entertainment disclosure.

But the paperwork doesn't explain why the consultants repeatedly traveled to Folsom while billing expenses associated with meetings in Sacramento.

The discrepancies also raise questions about what the High-Speed Rail Authority reviewed before approving the payment.

If the travel forms didn't identify where the consultants actually went, how did the state determine whether the expenses were legitimate?

The receipts reveal another late-night destination, this time across the country.

In May 2025, Prate and Butzin both billed travel to Washington, D.C., during the High Speed Rail 2025 conference, where Choudri was scheduled to speak on May 14, according to the conference agenda.

Just before 1 a.m. that morning, Prate expensed the first of two Lyft rides totaling roughly $60 from Shelly's Back Room , a Washington cigar lounge, to the Mayflower Hotel and back to the cigar lounge just before 1:30 a.m.

The records don't indicate who else was there.

Butzin's records raise a different question.

He billed more than $1300 for a May 13-16 trip to "Attend USHSR Annual Conference and Meetings with CHSRA/Industry Suppliers." The records include no receipts.

The inspector general's report revealed how requests from the CEO's office influenced travel approvals.

When a contract manager reminded a Denver-based legal consultant that he needed to explain his trips and obtain advance written approval, the consultant pushed back.

According to the email excerpt in the inspector general's report, Butzin argued that justifying travel wasn't his responsibility when the CEO requested his presence.

Butzin added that questioning the CEO's direction was inappropriate, "as other consultants in other Authority offices are learning the hard way."

The contract manager told investigators she was directed, primarily by the acting chief counsel, to approve travel expenses because the CEO had requested the trips.

The inspector general concluded that the CEO didn't have authority to override the state contract's travel requirements.

The report documents pressure surrounding travel approvals. It doesn't establish that anyone was fired or explicitly threatened with termination.

But sources inside the High-Speed Rail Authority say the concerns extend beyond consultant travel.

They describe a workplace where some consultants are perceived as having unusual influence because of their relationships with leadership, raising questions about whether employees feel empowered to challenge spending and other decisions.

The watchdog's findings provide documented examples of the tension between executive requests and the employees responsible for enforcing contract rules.

Expensive travel. Little advance scrutiny.

The inspector general's findings are especially significant when compared with Butzin's travel records.

The High-Speed Rail Authority also paid the Denver-based consultant approximately $86,500 in hourly travel pay, totaling over a quarter of a million dollars when combined with reimbursed expenses.

Separate receipts CBS California obtained document expensive flights and hotel stays, including one airfare of nearly $937 for a flight from Denver to Sacramento and one hotel night costing $587.

The expense records include airline tickets purchased shortly before departure. The inspector general found that Butzin frequently booked flights on the day of travel, creating a risk of higher costs.

Last-minute flights aren't necessarily wasteful. Executives sometimes schedule meetings with little notice, requiring consultants to travel on short notice.

But last-minute bookings can also cost significantly more.

The watchdog's findings raise a straightforward question.

If the authority didn't document why the travel was necessary or approve it in advance, how could it ensure taxpayers weren't paying more than they needed to?

Other emails show how quickly some executive-related requests were approved.

In one exchange, Prate told the authority that Choudri had requested that he accompany him on a trip beginning the following day.

The request went to High-Speed Rail's chief financial officer.

That doesn't establish that the travel was unnecessary.

But it shows how directly a request invoking the CEO could influence the approval process.

A quarter of a billion dollars in consultant payments. Who's watching?

The High-Speed Rail Authority prepared a presentation to respond to the Inspector General's investigation at Friday's board meeting.

The original version, uploaded early in the week, emphasized how little it spent on travel compared with its total consultant payments. The pie chart further highlights the scale of consultant spending.

Over just two fiscal years, the Authority paid four consulting contractors more than a quarter of a billion dollars. Only about $2 million was for travel.

The inspector general reviewed roughly half of that and found more than half was unallowable under state rules or contract terms.

According to whistleblowers, this points to a much bigger concern:

If the authority couldn't enforce basic travel-spending rules, who is overseeing the rest of the quarter-billion dollars?

But that slide was missing from the presentation the authority ultimately gave the board.

The revised version no longer discloses the total payments to those contractors.

In an email, a spokesperson said, "The information was streamlined to keep the focus clear for the Board and the public.

What are taxpayers getting for the money?

Since Ian Choudri became CEO in 2024, California's high-speed rail project has fallen further behind, even as the authority pays four major consulting contractors more than a quarter of a billion dollars over two fiscal years.

These are consultants. They're paid to provide legal advice, financial guidance, program management and engineering design. Their work helps shape the decisions about what gets built, how it gets built and what taxpayers will pay.

California created its High-Speed Rail Authority 30 years ago, in 1996. Nearly two decades have passed since voters approved billions in funding for a bullet train connecting San Francisco and Los Angeles.

Yet the state still hasn't laid a mile of high-speed rail track.

Meanwhile, a CBS California investigation found the High-Speed Rail Authority, under Choudri, repeatedly missed its own deadlines to purchase trains. Federal officials cited those failures when they withdrew $4 billion in funding.

As of October, no high-speed rail track had been laid, and the project's independent inspector general warns California could run out of money as soon as December 2027 unless it secures additional financing.

The authority says it is revising designs and changing the project's scope to reduce costs. The inspector general said much of the projected cost reduction reflected plans to build less, like reducing the plans from two tracks to one.

But in a separate review of the authority's 2026 business plan , the inspector general found that the project's schedule slipped nine months in less than a year.

Whistleblowers inside the authority question whether the promised savings account for the costs of further delays and additional consultant work.

That brings us back to the late-night rides from the CEO's home.

The receipts don't show who was present or what decisions, if any, were made or what discussions were had at the residence and nearby restaurants.

But whistleblowers warn of increasingly costly delays while California pays consultants a quarter of a billion dollars to help shape decisions, sometimes leading to more delays. They believe taxpayers deserve answers.

Who proposed the design changes? Who approved them? How much are consultants charging to revise the work? And do the projected savings outweigh the costs of delay?

The receipts reveal where the consultants went. The bigger question, say whistleblowers, is what taxpayers are getting in return.

Why is California paying high-speed rail consultants to fly to Sacramento when they promised they would be based in Sacramento?

In part two of our series, The Receipts, CBS California Investigates the money behind a $131 million engineering contract.

The firm promised its key personnel would relocate to Sacramento. But newly obtained receipts reveal three of the six are traveling in from out of state on the taxpayers' dime, while one senior consultant's billing rate increased nearly 23%.

The watchdog questioned more than $76,000 in travel expenses. Our investigation reveals the receipts.

[EDITORS NOTE: This story was updated to include new details following the High Speed Rail Board meeting on October 9, 2026.]
