articles.title: In 2019, Pink Floyd's David Gilmour auctioned his treasured guitars in a $21.5 million sale; the proceeds went to environmental lawyers working to tackle climate change and protect nature
articles.summary: For David Gilmour, guitars were never just instruments.
articles.body: For David Gilmour, guitars were never just instruments. They helped create some of Pink Floyd’s most recognisable music, shaping solos heard on albums such as The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall. Yet in 2019, the guitarist decided to part with more than 120 pieces from his personal collection, sending them to auction at Christie’s in New York. The sale brought in $21,490,750, and Gilmour donated the proceeds to ClientEarth, an environmental law charity working to tackle climate change and protect nature. Christie’s described the event as the most valuable musical instruments sale in auction history at the time. For Gilmour, the decision was not simply about finding new homes for cherished guitars. He hoped their next chapter could help support a future in which people could continue to make music on a liveable planet.A collection with a historyThe 126 guitars in the sale were not a random collection of instruments. Many had accompanied Gilmour through decades of recording and performance, becoming part of the sound and history of Pink Floyd. They included Fender Broadcasters, Esquires, Telecasters and Stratocasters, instruments he had chosen for their distinct qualities and kept over the years.The most famous was the 1969 Fender Stratocaster known as “The Black Strat.” Gilmour used it on landmark Pink Floyd albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall. When it sold for $3,975,000, it set a world auction record for a guitar, according to Christie’s.The sale also featured a guitar used on “Wish You Were Here,” along with instruments connected to Gilmour’s solo work and other Pink Floyd recordings. Each item carried a story that went beyond its make or model. For fans, the instruments offered a tangible link to the music; for collectors, they represented rare pieces of rock history.A record-breaking auctionChristie’s held the auction in New York on June 20, 2019. The collection sold in its entirety, raising $21,490,750, or about $21.5 million. The auction attracted bidders from 66 countries and ran for eight hours, reflecting the worldwide interest in Gilmour’s instruments.The Black Strat drew the most attention, but it was not the only guitar to command an extraordinary price. The sale established multiple records and became a landmark event for musical instruments at auction. Christie’s called it the largest and most comprehensive guitar sale of its kind.Gilmour had announced before the auction that all proceeds would go to ClientEarth. The decision gave the event a purpose beyond collecting and memorabilia. Every bid contributed to an environmental law organisation whose work is often less visible than frontline conservation, but which seeks to change the rules and decisions that affect the natural world.Why ClientEarth?ClientEarth uses law to address environmental problems, including climate change and the protection of nature. Rather than operating as a traditional advocacy group alone, it works with lawyers, scientists and policy experts to challenge harmful practices and strengthen environmental protections, as per reports.In its June 2019 announcement, ClientEarth said Gilmour had donated the money raised from the collection to support its efforts to tackle the climate crisis. The organisation’s chief executive, James Thornton, called the gift an extraordinary boost to its work using the law to address environmental problems. Gilmour explained his motivation in a statement shared by ClientEarth. He described the global climate crisis as humanity’s greatest challenge and said he hoped the sale would help the charity use the law to bring about real change. He added that he wanted a civilised world that would continue for future generations, where guitars could still be played and songs could still be sung.The connection between music and environmental protection was personal as well as symbolic. Gilmour’s instruments had helped produce work that reached millions of people. By giving away the auction proceeds, he turned that cultural legacy into support for an organisation seeking lasting legal and policy change.Letting the guitars move onGilmour later said the guitars had been very good to him, but that it was time for them to move on. The sale meant parting with instruments that had accompanied him through important moments in his career, including the creation and performance of music that remains part of Pink Floyd’s legacy.For the buyers, the guitars became prized possessions. For ClientEarth, their sale provided resources for environmental work. The auction transformed objects with individual histories into a single, substantial donation.That decision also brought attention to the role of environmental law. Climate change and biodiversity loss can feel too large for individual action, but legal challenges and policy changes can influence how governments and businesses respond. ClientEarth’s work focuses on using the law as a tool to make those systems more accountable.A legacy beyond the stageThe 2019 auction stands out because it joined two worlds that rarely meet so visibly: rock history and environmental law. The Black Strat alone brought in nearly $4 million, while the entire collection raised more than $21 million for a charity focused on protecting the planet.The sale did not solve the climate crisis, and Gilmour did not present it as a complete answer. Instead, it was a substantial contribution to the work of an organisation he believed could help create change. His hope was that the proceeds would support a future in which the natural world, and the people who depend on it, could endure.For music fans, the guitars remain part of the story behind some of Pink Floyd’s most influential recordings. For ClientEarth, they became the means to fund legal work on climate and nature. And for Gilmour, the auction offered a way to let treasured instruments move on while giving their next chapter a purpose beyond music.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Eight men arrested days after early release from jail
articles.summary: Some are held for breaching criminal orders, others for robbery or domestic violence, police say.
articles.body:
Eight men have been arrested by Greater Manchester Police days after leaving prison under the government's early release scheme.

About 700 prisoners from across the country were released early on 1 October in a bid to tackle overcrowding, with about 50 of them being from Greater Manchester.

GMP confirmed that five men had been arrested for breaches of criminal orders, including a domestic abuse prevention order, and others were held on suspicion of robbery, drug offences and domestic violence.

In response, the Ministry of justice (MOJ) said: "We inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. If we had failed to act, the police would have been forced to halt arrests."

Under the first phase of the early release scheme , offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months were eligible to be released after serving one third of their sentence.

The move, which will see a further 2,500 prisoners released across the country by the end of the year, is due to the prison system running on 98.2% capacity.

The MOJ said: "We will never jeopardise public safety. That is why we are putting thousands more Neighbourhood Police officers on to our streets, upping police funding to £18.5bn and taking investment in the probation service to record levels.

"To manage offenders out on licence, we are rolling out the toughest-ever controls, including world-first restriction zones, the largest expansion of electronic tagging, and giving victims a say in licence conditions."

GMP Deputy Chief Constable Terry Wood said the force had been working "closely" with partners so that "robust plans are in place to ensure offenders are adhering to their conditions" adding that any breaches "will be, and are being - enforced by GMP".

"As with any offending in Greater Manchester, where there is a report of a crime we will respond promptly to take positive action to protect victims and pursue criminals," he added.

articles.title: Sara Sharif's grandfather granted guardianship of her siblings in Pakistan
articles.summary: All five children have been living with him in Pakistan since 2023, when 10-year-old Sara was murdered.
articles.body:
Sara Sharif's paternal grandfather has been granted guardianship of her siblings by a court in Pakistan.

The decision comes after years of legal limbo following the murder of 10-year-old Sara by her father and stepmother in 2023.

All five children, who are now aged between 16 and four, have been living in Pakistan since 2023. They were asked to speak to the judge in court, where the eldest said they were comfortable and the siblings were settled.

Sara's grandfather, Muhammed Sharif, told the BBC he was relieved to be granted guardianship after three years of legal battles, saying his hope is that the children "stay healthy" and receive "a good education".

"It is my responsibility to ensure they get the best possible education and care," he said.

When told by the judge that the grandfather would become their guardian, the eldest child responded saying "that's all good".

The five children have been in Pakistan since August 2023, when they were brought to the country by Sara's father, stepmother and uncle after Sara was killed.

The family was in hiding for weeks before the children were discovered by police at the grandfather's house. They were initially put into state childcare.

The adults flew back to the UK and were arrested at the airport. Sara's father Urfan Sharif and stepmother Beinash Batool were found guilty of Sara's murder. Sharif was sentenced to a minimum of 40 years in prison and Batool received a minimum of 33 years.

Her uncle, Faisal Malik, was found guilty of causing or allowing her death and given a 16-year sentence.

Sara had been hooded, burned and beaten during a "campaign of torture" that lasted two years before her body was found at the family home in Woking, Surrey.

In Pakistan, Sara's grandfather was given temporary custody of her siblings in October 2023. All but the youngest are now attending school in Pakistan, the grandfather has said.

Speaking following Saturday's decision, their grandfather said "we will help them to return to a normal life".

"Hardships can happen to any person at any time, at any place," he said, adding "we will move forward".

Muhammed said that he speaks to his son Urfan once a week or every second week. "Not with the children, not regarding the case. Nothing else, just to ask about each other's well-being".

When asked about allegations that he had helped hide the three adults, Muhammed said they had left soon after arriving in Jhelum and that at the time he had told them to return to the UK.

The children's grandfather added that the siblings will keep their British passports and go back to the UK "when they reach the right age".

The children were made wards of court in England, and Surrey County council had been trying to bring them back through the courts in Pakistan.

Their grandfather has been fighting for them to stay with him. Surrey withdrew from the case in June, saying it had no ability to pursue the application in Pakistan, as English proceedings are coming to an end.

A final decision on their guardianship had not been made in Pakistan's courts until Saturday.

articles.title: When streets become a workplace: Gaza workers convert tents into offices
articles.summary: A real estate crisis in Gaza has forced professionals to use tents as surgeries and offices.
articles.body:
Khan Younis, Gaza – Dr Mohammed al-Khalidi, a specialist in prosthetics and orthotics, sits in a modest tent in al-Mawasi, southern Gaza. It has been his place of work since his clinic on al-Bahr Street in Rafah was destroyed by Israeli bombing in April 2024. His second and third clinics in Khan Younis’s Old City, southern Gaza, were subsequently destroyed by Israel in May 2025.

After this triple heartbreaking setback, al-Khalidi salvaged whatever medical equipment he could find and moved into his new office, a tent, where he has received patients for the past two years.

This transitory space reflects a new reality in Gaza since Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave began in October 2023. Offices, clinics and shops have been wiped out in waves of Israeli air raids over the past three years, leaving professionals to conduct their work from tents or on the road.

This phenomenon emerged in December 2023 following the displacement of Khan Younis residents to a narrow strip of coastal land between their hometown and Deir el-Balah.

After a ceasefire, repeatedly broken by Israel, was announced for the enclave in October 2025, more of these tent offices, surgeries and shops emerged across Gaza as professionals sought to continue their practices.

Working within these canvas confines presents multiple challenges for al-Khalidi. There is limited space, unreliable electricity, and the intense heat and loud noises to deal with.

The setting bears little resemblance to his previous practice in a bricks-and-mortar office, but he still feels this arrangement is better than suspending services altogether.

There is a massive need for prosthetics in Gaza, where between 5,000 and 6,000 people have undergone amputations between October 2023 and October 2025.

“Working from a temporary space is nothing like working in a fully equipped clinic, but for me, it is better than stopping the service altogether,” al-Khalidi told Al Jazeera.

“Patients who need prosthetic limbs or orthotic devices cannot always wait until conditions return to normal. Some have lost a limb during the war, while others need follow-up care or adjustments to devices they rely on in their daily lives.”

More than four-in-five buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed since Israel’s genocidal war began in 2023, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS), creating a real estate crisis.

The lack of office space has seen rental prices reach unaffordable levels for most Gaza professionals. But resilience, necessity, and duty have encouraged Palestinians to find solutions to this situation. Tents are now where lawyers meet clients, doctors treat patients, and traders sell their wares.

After Omar al-Tawashi, a civil engineer and construction auditor, saw his office destroyed in an Israeli air strike in August 2024, he began work from his home in July 2025. But that too met the same fate, so he shifted operations to a tent in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, to continue his work.

“My move to a tent was not a professional choice. It was a direct result of the destruction of the place where I used to work, compounded by the rental crisis, which made finding an alternative office extremely difficult,” he said.

“In some cases, rents have risen to more than 10 times their pre-war levels, making a new office beyond my means”.

The tent is not a suitable environment for his engineering work, but there is no alternative for al-Tawashi.

“There is heat, cold and noise, and none of the privacy needed when discussing projects or reviewing technical files,” Omar said. “But stopping work would mean losing my source of income”.

In the crowded market in Nuseirat camp, central Gaza, accountant Mahmoud Shaheen receives clients inside a small tent amid the sound of neighbouring vendors and passers-by.

Shaheen was once responsible for a Gaza-based company’s accounts, but the office was destroyed in an Israeli air strike in November 2025.

“Moving to a tent was not so much a professional choice as a response to a reality imposed by the war,” he told Al Jazeera.

With the start of the new school year in Gaza last month, tents have been pitched across the country as substitutes for schools destroyed in Israeli air raids or converted into refuges for the displaced.

Teacher Palestine Hussein has been forced to adapt to this new reality. She previously taught English at an educational centre in Bureij in central Gaza, which she had spent years building.

It was destroyed in seconds when an Israeli air raid destroyed the educational facility, so she now teaches children from a tent at al-Balata, a camp for displaced Palestinians in Nuseirat.

There is a lack of seats for the students, ventilation, or protection from the noise and heat. But despite these challenges, Hussein is determined to provide children in the camp with some form of education.

“Although the tent may appear to be a temporary place, to me it represents an attempt to hold on to what remains of my profession and rebuild my dream from scratch, even with the most basic resources,” Hussein told Al Jazeera.

Trader Khalil al-Tahrawi saw his clothing store in Nuseirat destroyed by Israeli bombing in October 2023. After salvaging surviving merchandise from his destroyed shop, he displayed his goods – mostly men’s T-shirts and jeans – at a small tent in the Nuseirat market.

He pays $350 a month in rent for the small patch of pavement to sell the clothing, which he removes every night to protect them from thieves.

“This routine makes the work even more difficult and consumes my time and energy,” al-Tahrawi told Al Jazeera.

Repeated power cuts, unreliable internet and shortages of equipment have complicated efforts by Gaza’s business community to rebuild during this period of a relative decrease in bombing.

Customers, too, are changing their consumption patterns, heading to certain towns or camps for a particular good or service. Often what they find are prices more inflated than during Israel’s siege on Gaza before Israel’s genocidal war.

One customer, Mohammed Zweid, a 24-year-old IT worker, looks through a market in Nuseirat. “Accessing professionals in tents and temporary spaces is better than having no service at all,” he told Al Jazeera. “The transformation has changed not only where services are provided, but also how they are experienced.”

articles.title: Rare coin bearing face of king with infamous nickname unearthed after 1,000 years
articles.summary: Marking the northernmost find of its kind, a 1,000-year-old Anglo-Saxon coin depicting King Ethelred the Unready was unearthed in the Shetland Islands.
articles.body: Archaeologists in Scotland recently uncovered an Anglo-Saxon coin dating back 1,000 years — minted under a king known as "the Unready." The coin was unearthed during an excavation in Nesting, a coastal community in Scotland's eastern Shetland Islands, according to Jam Press. Pictures show a thick, greenish-brown patina covering its surface, though some of the original markings remain visible. TEEN STUMBLES ON MYSTERIOUS COIN FROM LEGENDARY CITY, PUZZLING ARCHAEOLOGISTS OVER ITS JOURNEY The excavation was originally conducted to investigate prehistoric structures threatened by coastal erosion, according to Archaeology Shetland. The archaeological investigation included an examination of nearby Iron Age structures. The artifact was minted between 991 and 997 A.D., Jam Press noted. The coin's face depicts King Ethelred the Unready, who ruled England from 978 to 1013 A.D. DISCOVERY BENEATH SOCCER FIELD REVEALS MASSIVE MEDIEVAL CONVENT LOST FOR CENTURIES Ethelred, best known for his failed attempts to fend off Viking invasions, was eventually driven from the throne by Danish king Swein Forkbeard. He regained power in 1014 and ruled until his death in 1016 — making him the longest-reigning Anglo-Saxon monarch. Elinor Graham, an archaeologist from the University of Aberdeen, was on vacation in Shetland when she participated in the excavation, according to Jam Press. MAN SEARCHING WITH METAL DETECTOR UNEARTHS MASSIVE VIKING AGE FORTUNE, SHATTERING RECORDS "This is exactly how I wanted to spend my holiday," Graham said. She added, "The writing on the coin is still so sharp, and we knew immediately that it was extremely rare, actually unique, in this context." "We knew immediately that it was extremely rare, actually unique, in this context." The discovery could offer clues about ancient trade routes between Viking-controlled Shetland and Anglo-Saxon England, though researchers have not ruled out the possibility that the coin was taken during a Norse raid. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Graham said another Anglo-Saxon coin had previously been discovered at Old Scatness, an archaeological site in southern Shetland; the latest find, though, marks the northernmost discovery of its kind. The coin may have reached Shetland through trade with England, though researchers have not ruled out the possibility it might have been taken as loot during a raid. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Scotland's Treasure Trove Unit will determine whether the artifact should be offered to a museum. Graham said she hopes the coin will eventually be added to the collections at the Shetland Museum and Archives, Jam Press reported. She said the discovery suggests the area may once have been home to a "well-connected cosmopolitan community" with trading links to Anglo-Saxon England. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "It's an area with a huge amount of history through the Bronze Age, the Iron Age, the early medieval period and into the Viking Norse period," Graham said. The ancient coin is one of many that have surfaced across the United Kingdom. Earlier this year, archaeologists uncovered a nearly 1,750-year-old Roman coin during a railway construction project in England. articles.title: Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’?
articles.summary: Fighting is intensifying between Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebel group.
articles.body:
Fighting continues to intensify in Yemen as the internationally recognised government forces push a military offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, which controls part of the country.

Speaking at the United Nations Security Council on Friday, the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, said the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”.

Government forces are particularly looking to retake the important Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital trading chokepoint that has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have all but halted shipping.

At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations.

More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in September, the UN’s migration agency (IOM), said.

Fierce battles across several fronts have prompted concerns from rights groups that Yemen has essentially returned to civil war after the relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014.

Amid the US-Iran war, Yemen’s worst fighting in years threatens to destabilise the region further, experts say. Here’s what we know:

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea. Riyadh has increasingly relied on it for oil exports amid the US-Iran war, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz.

On Sunday, the Yemeni government announced the start of the operation “Dawn of Yemen”, which aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa.

On Saturday, it said it had conducted more than 2,750 precision strikes during military operations over the previous 24 hours, resulting in the “neutralisation” of more than 1,400 Houthi fighters.

The spokesperson for the armed forces, Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, said in a statement carried by Saba news agency that the operations also targeted high-value military assets deep within Houthi-held territory.

He added that ground forces “successfully” breached Houthi defences, recaptured operationally significant positions, secured their field gains and continued to advance the offensive according to operational plans.

The Bab al-Mandeb strait emerged as yet another front in the US-Israel war on Iran when the Houthis declared a blockade on ships linked to Saudi Arabia in July.

While the Houthis said that was in retaliation for ongoing Saudi blockades on Yemen, analysts viewed the move as calculated to provide more leverage for Iran amid on-and-off negotiations with the US – a close ally of Riyadh.

Battles are now raging around the strategic southern cities of Mocha and Dubhab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb. The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides currently claim control of the shipping lanes.

The Houthis, who have developed sophisticated weapons systems, including ballistic missiles, have also targeted Saudi Arabia with missile and drone attacks. On Friday, Saudi Arabia’s aviation authorities said three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, had been killed and several others wounded in Houthi strikes on the international airport in Riyadh – the first such deaths in the kingdom since fighting resumed. Several airlines suspended flights.

The coalition forces also heavily bombarded Sanaa, on Friday, with several injuries reported, including a child. Both sides are also fighting to control Taiz.

Civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis took control of Sanaa and imposed their own government in the capital. The seizure came amid dissatisfaction with the ruling government and following a revolution three years earlier.

A coalition of armed forces and local armed groups backed by Saudi Arabia launched military operations and restored the internationally recognised government in Aden. Fighting resulted in the deaths of between 150,000 and 227,000 people, while millions were displaced.

While the Houthis controlled much of the north, the Yemeni government controlled the southern regions.

A UN-brokered truce in 2022 saw a lull in fighting and allowed aid to reach the deprived population, which has faced famine since 2016.

In 2023, the Houthis, who form part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” alliance of proxy armed groups, began disrupting shipping in the Red Sea in response to Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip. In March this year, the Houthis fired missiles at Israel amid the war on Iran, officially entering the US-Israel war with Iran which began in February.

Tensions escalated when the group declared a naval blockade of Saudi ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July, shattering the relative calm in the country since 2022. It followed the announcement with a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back Yemeni coalition forces from the strategic port city.

In September, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.

On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, leader of the Yemeni government’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a military offensive to “restore state authority”.

Analysts say the scale of fighting means Yemen has fallen back into civil war as both sides come under scrutiny for targeting civilians.

As the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, declared that the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”, civilians, including women and children, are the ones bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.

The envoy stressed the need for the UNSC to support urgent mediation once more, although analysts have pointed out that recent gains by Yemeni government forces could mean they are more determined to push through the ongoing offensive, rather than agree to a settlement.

But “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now”, Grundberg warned.

Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, said: “It is beginning to resemble the 2015 Saudi-led coalition war on Yemen, when Sanaa and various other provinces were attacked relentlessly around the clock.”

A number of sites in Sanaa have been targeted, he said, including Sanaa International Airport. Several industrial facilities, including a chips factory in the north and a sponge factory in the south, have also been hit.

At least four telecommunications infrastructure sites have been struck in the capital and throughout areas controlled by the Houthi movement. Mount Attan in Sanaa was also hit by 10 air raids.

Mawry reported that, according to Saudi coalition officials, strikes have destroyed 136 military targets in areas under Houthi control, including military sites, launch pads and radars belonging to the Houthi group.

“Meanwhile, the Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of targeting public infrastructure and telecommunications facilities, warning that the campaign risks plunging the country back into a humanitarian crisis similar to the one experienced from 2015 to 2022,” Mawry said.

Will the United States take action in Yemen?

The US, which has previously indicated that it does not want to get involved in the Yemen conflict, nevertheless on Friday called on the Houthis to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, while demanding that Iran end its support for the group.

Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Yemen, Jeff Bartos, the US ambassador to the UN for Management and Reform, said Washington was “gravely concerned” by the Houthis’ recent escalation, including attacks on civilian infrastructure and airports.

“The pattern remains unmistakable. The Houthis act as instruments of Tehran to threaten freedom of navigation, undermine regional stability, and terrorise innocent civilians,” Bartos said.

“We demand that the Houthis cease their attacks against the legitimate governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia and we demand that Iran cease all support to the Houthis,” he added.

articles.title: Abbas postpones Palestinian legislative elections to September 2027
articles.summary: November 2026 vote delayed; joint presidential and legislative elections set for next year, president says in decree.
articles.body:
President Mahmoud Abbas has postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council for almost another year.

According to the decree, legislative elections planned for next month will be combined with a presidential vote and set for September 11, 2027, Wafa, the official Palestinian news agency, said on Saturday.

The long-awaited parliamentary vote was originally set for November 28, with a presidential election expected in early 2027.

The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met on Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote.

The Palestine Liberation Organization’s (PLO) Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in occupied East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.

Israeli interference, including military raids, settlement expansion and settler violence in the occupied West Bank, has made a fair vote in November impossible, Wafa reported.

The agency also cited Israel’s systemic withholding of Palestinian tax revenues and its restrictions on electoral candidates and international observers entering Gaza and occupied East Jerusalem, as reasons.

As for Gaza, it said that the lack of progress on reconstruction and on deploying an international stabilisation force factored into the decision as well.

The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority’s (PA) credibility among Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.

On Friday, the Israeli Minister of Foreign Affairs, Gideon Saar, accused Abbas of “fooling the international community” by planning to cancel promised elections.

A source told the AFP news agency on Thursday that Palestinian factions, including Abbas’s Palestinian National Liberation Movement – also known as the Fatah party – had agreed to hold a “national dialogue” before legislative elections and that they wanted to postpone the vote.

The last parliamentary elections held in the Palestinian territories were in 2006, when Hamas defeated Fatah, which dominates the PA. The split led to factional fighting and Hamas later seized control of Gaza.

Ninety-year-old Abbas won the last presidential election in 2005. His term should have ended in 2009, but he has ruled by decree since then. In June, he signed a decree calling for the presidential election to be held in early 2027.

Mustafa Barghouti, secretary-general of the Palestinian National Initiative party, told Al Jazeera there is great disappointment among the Palestinian people over Abbas’s decision to postpone the elections.

“At this moment, everything is concentrated in the hands of the executive authority,” he said.

“There is no independent judiciary, no parliament, that can issue laws and legislations,” Barghouti added, saying it is “totally unacceptable” that Palestinians have been denied elections for two decades.

“There is a great need for reform from the perspective of the Palestinian people.”

articles.title: Why is the US sanctioning the International Criminal Court?
articles.summary: The sanctions targeting the ICC, which prosecutes humanitarian crimes, are the latest move by the US against the court.
articles.body:
The United States has sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), hours after one of its former judges was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in what the Nobel committee said was, in part, a show of support for institutions under attack.

South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who is currently a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also in The Hague, was announced winner of the prize on Friday.

Nobel Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice,” the committee said.

The US move follows sanctions it has already imposed this year on judges and other personnel at the ICC.

On Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the latest set of US sanctions targeting the ICC, this time focusing on the court itself, which was established in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” he said in a video shared on social media.

The Trump administration claims that the ICC has gone beyond its remit by pursuing non-member countries. In 2024, the Trump administration condemned the court when it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for suspected war crimes in Gaza. It also previously opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan.

The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction. However, abuses committed by citizens of non-statute states in ICC territories or countries can still be prosecuted.

“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement, adding that if the US allies failed to “rein in the court”, the US would “continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”.

What other sanctions has the US imposed on the ICC?

These sanctions are just the latest in the US’s campaign against the ICC. Previous measures have targeted dozens of ICC judges and prosecutors , the UN special rapporteur for Palestine, Francesca Albanese, and Palestinian rights groups which have provided evidence of war crimes committed by Israel to the court.

In August, ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior lawyer Abdoulaye Sey were also sanctioned by the US, in what Rubio said was the US’s unwavering mission to protect Americans from this sham of a court”.

Any assets they hold in the US are frozen, and US companies are limited in conducting transactions with them.

>What do the latest sanctions mean in practice?

The sanctions targeting the court could see companies that provide services to it penalised. They will also freeze any ICC assets held in US territories.

However, they have given US companies a six-month grace period to wrap up any existing business with the court. There are also some other exemptions allowing for certain transactions.

William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London, told Al Jazeera that the court has been “developing a plan B” to get around potential sanctions for more than a year.

This includes migrating to European alternatives to US software, and ending its relationship with insurance company Axa, which does business with the US.

“How significant this will be remains to be seen,” he said. “Obviously for the institution, it’s going to complicate things considerably.”

“What Trump is trying to do is to make the world safe for American and Israeli war criminals,” Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University and former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera.

The ICC itself released a statement condemning the US move, which it said was an attempt to “obstruct the course of justice” and intimidate those who work or cooperate with the court.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” it said, calling on its 125 states parties to take action to ensure it can continue its work.

“History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it added.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply alarmed” by the decision, adding that it was “a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice”.

The foreign ministers of the UK, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan all said they “strongly disagree” with the sanctions, and warned of the significant impact they would have on the court.

Netanyahu thanked Trump for his leadership on social media, and accused the ICC of being a “political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide”.

Is the US eroding the system of international law?

The US targeting of the ICC threatens the rule of law, as international courts and tribunals must be able to operate without the threat of sanctions.

The US itself has repeatedly ignored international law under President Trump. Its joint attack on Iran with Israel in February was criticised by observers as being in violation of both US law and Article 2(4) of the UN Charter , while the US military abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from Caracas in January was also condemned as illegal.

The Trump administration has also launched strikes against alleged drug smuggling boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific, killing more than 200 people in what UN human rights experts warn are “ extrajudicial and unlawful “.

Under Trump, the US has also pulled out of international organisations and agreements, from the Iran nuclear deal (the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action) and the Paris Climate Agreement during Trump’s first term, to the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, more recently.

“What Trump is doing is obstructing justice,” Roth said of the ICC sanctions. “If you look at Article 70 of the Rome Statute, it makes it a crime to intimidate or threaten court officials because of their official duties.”

“But the court remains strong, it is very capable of doing its work,” he said, adding, “there’s important work for the court to do to protect victims in places like Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, Afghanistan, the Philippines. This is work that should continue, and it will.”

articles.title: Third school attack in Poland in a week sparks safety concerns
articles.summary: A third attack at a Polish school in less than a week took place on Saturday, when a 21-year-old woman injured three people at an educational institution
articles.body: A third attack at a Polish school in less than a week took place on Saturday, when a 21-year-old woman injured three people at an educational institution in Warsaw, police said.The woman allegedly used a “dangerous object” to attack a 17-year-old girl, injuring two other people aged 17 and 24 in the process, Jakub Filipiak, a Warsaw police spokesperson, told The Associated Press. None of the injuries was life-threatening.The incident came as authorities intensified security measures across Poland following two school attacks earlier in the week that left one person dead and several others injured, including children. Police said on Saturday that they had detained 76 people across the country and inspected nearly 50,000 schools to prevent further violence, according to the AP.On Friday, schools nationwide tightened security, with 59 institutions suspending classes, many parents keeping their children at home and police patrols deployed at educational facilities. School authorities also introduced additional precautions, including placing more staff at entrances and conducting voluntary backpack checks.“There will be no compromise here. The safety of the youth is the most important thing,” Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said.The heightened alert followed two violent incidents in the central province of Mazovia. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student at a vocational school attacked fellow students, teachers and passersby with a sharp object, injuring nine people before fleeing. He was arrested nearby.The following day, a 15-year-old attacked his former school in the same province, killing a school custodian and injuring two others in a knife attack. The teenager, who reportedly wore a camera to record his actions, was eventually overpowered by school director Krzysztof Ochmanski.Both attacks were carried out by Polish nationals and shocked a country where school violence involving minors has emerged as a growing concern.By Thursday night, rumours circulating in parents’ online groups and mainstream media suggested that the attacks might have been coordinated and that further violence could occur on Friday, which was dubbed “bloody Friday”.Authorities said those detained during the security operation included a 14-year-old boy from central Warsaw who was found carrying a knife with a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers. A 16-year-old from another Warsaw district was found with a butterfly knife in his school backpack. Others were detained over allegedly posting pictures of knives online, threatening fellow students or making threats against schools.The government said it had found no evidence so far of an ongoing online challenge encouraging school attacks. Authorities have also not officially confirmed any link between the two earlier incidents, and both alleged perpetrators remain in custody.The attacks have prompted parents across Poland to seek ways to discuss school violence with their children. Officials have said enhanced security measures will remain in place and crisis-response training will be organised.The liberal government has also pledged to renew efforts to pass legislation aimed at blocking harmful online content.Prime Minister Donald Tusk stated that, “If that juvenile attacker had streamed the crime online today, we would have been unable to block that content because we have not been given that legal tool.”Recounting his confrontation with the 15-year-old attacker, Ochmanski said the teenager appeared to grasp the gravity of his actions at one point and indicated that he no longer wanted to continue.“Once I had established contact, he asked me for help,” Ochmanski said. “It got to the point where he wanted a hug.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Drone strike by Sudan paramilitary kills 41 near Ethiopian border, rights group says
articles.summary: Eight children are said to be among those killed by the strike, which hit a gathering of displaced people.
articles.body:
A drone attack by Sudan's paramilitary forces has killed 41 people in the country's Blue Nile region bordering Ethiopia, a rights group has said.

The strike by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted a camp for displaced people in the state's Abu Shandi area on Friday, Emergency Lawyers said.

The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said it was "appalled by horrifying reports". It said initial reports suggested most of the casualties were women and children.

The Sudanese army and paramilitary forces including the RSF have been locked in a power struggle since 2023, a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than 14 million from their homes.

It has also created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with millions of people needing medical help.

The army controls much of Sudan's central and eastern regions, while the RSF is headquartered in the western region of Darfur and also controls areas in the south.

Both sides have been accused of using drone attacks.

Ocha said in a statement that the area reportedly struck on Friday had been "under sustained atttack in recent weeks, displacing thousands of civilians and exposing many more to grave harm".

articles.title: Delhi protests: SC to hear plea seeking contempt action against authorities on Sunday
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court will hear on Sunday a plea seeking contempt proceedings against authorities for allegedly violating its October 9 direction
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court will hear on Sunday a plea seeking contempt proceedings against authorities for allegedly violating its October 9 direction on maintaining metro and train services during protests in Delhi.The plea will be heard on Sunday by a bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, according to the Supreme Court’s cause list. It seeks contempt proceedings against Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and DMRC chairperson D Thara.Filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi through advocate Chand Qureshi, the petition alleges that the authorities deliberately failed to comply with the court’s directions. “This brutal assault on the fundamental rights of the citizens and sheer disregard to the orders of this court amounts to deliberate, intentional attempt on the part of Delhi Metro, Delhi Police and the Union government which must be dealt with an iron hand,” it said, as quoted by PTI.The dispute stems from restrictions imposed ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed demonstration at Jantar Mantar on October 10. The party and student organisations had called for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the Election Commission.Ahead of the protest, the closure of 57 metro stations and cancellation of trains to Delhi were challenged in a separate petition before the Supreme Court. On October 9, a bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Bagchi and Mohana directed the Centre to ensure there was no “complete prohibition” on metro and train movement into the capital the following day.The court acknowledged that law enforcement agencies could take steps to prevent unruly movement but said citizens should not face undue harassment. It also cautioned against bringing all transport services to a halt because of the proposed demonstration.Delhi nevertheless witnessed extensive security restrictions on Saturday. Police denied permission for the gathering, citing procedural and law-and-order concerns, and deployed barricades and checkpoints across parts of the capital. Restrictions on transport and mobile internet in some areas added to the disruption, while opposition leaders, students, lawyers and activists were detained as they attempted to join the protest.The police action also prompted separate legal interventions. Chief Justice Surya Kant communicated to authorities that lawyers detained while peacefully protesting outside the Supreme Court should be released, following an urgent letter from the Supreme Court Bar Association. The association had said several advocates were taken to the Yamuna Sports Complex.CPM general secretary MA Baby also moved the Supreme Court challenging restrictions imposed ahead of the protest, including curbs on metro services and mobile internet connectivity. Trinamool Congress spokesperson Saket Gokhale separately approached the Delhi High Court’s acting chief justice, seeking suo motu intervention over transport restrictions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Woman injures three people in third Poland school knife attack in a week
articles.summary: Polish police had already deployed to schools after a female caretaker was killed and several others injured in two earlier attacks in two days.
articles.body:
A woman has been arrested after injuring three people in a third knife attack recorded at schools in Poland this week.

The 21-year-old used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw, police told news agencies PAP and AP.

It comes a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.

A Warsaw police spokesperson said they could not confirm whether the latest incident was related to the two previous attacks.

Authorities told local media that the 17-year-old injured on Saturday had been taken to hospital, but her condition was not life-threatening.

Two other women aged 17 and 24, who had gone in to submit enrolment documents, were also injured, Poland's state news agency reported.

Police told local media that the suspected attacker was a student at the school and initial findings suggested that she did not know the three victims.

Schools in Poland had been stepping up security following knife attacks at schools across the country on 7 and 8 October. Polish police said they had detained 76 people after deploying to schools across the country.

"When it comes to the safety of Polish children and peace in our schools, there is no room for compromise," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said ahead of the operation.

Local media, citing a police spokesperson, reported authorities had information to suggest incidents this past week could be related to an internet challenge.

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.

A day later, a 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".

articles.title: Pope Leo declares death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as his native U.S. plans to livestream execution
articles.summary: ROME — Pope Leo XIV on Saturday declared capital punishment “inadmissible” as he marked the World Day Against the Death Penalty and his native United States announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.
articles.body: ROME — Pope Leo XIV on Saturday declared capital punishment “inadmissible” as he marked the World Day Against the Death Penalty and his native United States announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. In a post on X, the American pope quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by Pope Francis that the death penalty attacks the inherent dignity of a human being. “The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” read the post under Leo’s official handle, @Pontifex. “Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.” The post ended with the hashtag #NoDeathPenalty. The U.S. Defense Department announced Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base, will be livestreamed. Hasan, scheduled to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. Leo didn’t refer specifically to the planned execution, or the botched lethal injection in Tennessee last week that has revived debate over the death penalty in the United States. Saturday is World Day Against the Death Penalty, and it is common for the pope’s official social media accounts to post messages marking such commemorations. But Leo’s post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said explicitly that the planned U.S. public execution was “unacceptable.” Pope Francis declared capital punishment ‘inadmissible’ Pope Francis in 2018 amended official Catholic teaching to declare capital punishment “inadmissible” in all circumstances. Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of church teaching, said the church didn’t exclude recourse to capital punishment “if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against the unjust aggressor.” Past popes had upheld that position, though St. John Paul II began urging an end to the practice and stressed that guilty people were just as deserving of dignity as innocent ones. Like Francis before him, Leo has made visiting prisons a key part of his papal travel in a bid to give a message of hope to inmates and underscore their inherent dignity, that God loves them and that there is always a chance for redemption. “If any of you fear being abandoned by everyone, know that God will never abandon you, and that the church will stand by your side,” Leo told inmates at the notorious Bata prison in Equatorial Guinea during his visit in April. Leo is to visit a prison in Buenos Aires during his upcoming tour through Latin America. Speaking specifically about the United States, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said the planned livestreamed execution was “truly incomprehensible” and “unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle.” “The Church’s position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent—,” Parolin said in comments carried by Vatican News. “It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don’t know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods.” The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed “shock” and “great sorrow” at the Pentagon’s plans. “In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said in a statement Friday. “The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people.”

articles.title: Several injured in fresh attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport
articles.summary: The US embassy says it is "aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport", which come days after Yemen's Houthis said they had struck it.
articles.body:
Several people have been injured in another attack on an international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, authorities say, days after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have carried out similar strikes on the hub.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were suspended on Saturday after the attack, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said in a statement.

More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to news agency Reuters, citing an eyewitness.

The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport" and urged American citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.

The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudis including a pilot were killed in two attacks on the airport by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior. Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.

A source at a local hospital told AFP that dozens of people had been wounded in Saturday's attack.

"I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running," an eyewitness who said they had been at gate 401 in the domestic terminal told the news agency.

Western embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens away from the airport, while the UK Foreign Office told British nationals to stay away "until the airport is secure and to monitor the advice of the Saudi authorities".

Several Gulf airlines said they had cancelled their flights to and from the airport, with Kuwait Airways citing the "security situation" there.

All flights to Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled, aviation tracker Flightradar shows.

Doctors had been asked to report to hospitals to address the situation, a medical source told AFP.

"We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'," the medical source told the agency.

The suspected attack comes during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.

The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.

The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

But the informal truce began to unravel in July.

The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

articles.body:

The suspect also ended up hurting two other people, aged 17 and 24 respectively, he said.

“One person was injured and transported to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. Two other bystanders also sustained injuries but did not require hospitalisation,” Filipiak added.

The police did not identify the educational institution, but said it was open on a Saturday because it is a higher education establishment. The attacker did not know any of the victims, the police said.

National Wyborcza newspaper identified the institution as TEB Edukacja, a school that gives post-secondary education. The suspect studied at this school, according to national media reports.

The attack came after police on Saturday said they detained 76 people across Poland and checked nearly 50,000 schools nationwide as part of efforts to prevent further violence following two school attacks earlier in the week.

On Friday, schools across Poland stepped up security, with some suspending classes, many parents keeping children at home and police patrols deployed to educational institutions after two attacks at schools earlier in the week left one person dead and several others wounded, including children.

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the Mazovian province in central Poland attacked fellow students, teachers and passersby with a sharp object, injuring nine people before fleeing and being arrested nearby.

The following day, a 15-year-old killed a school custodian and wounded two others in a knife attack at his former school in the same province.

The assaults, both carried out by Polish nationals, shocked a country where school violence by minors is a new phenomenon.

By Thursday night, rumours that the attacks were coordinated and that there would be more on the culmination day dubbed “bloody Friday” were being shared in parents’ online groups and by mainstream media.

Fifty-nine schools pre-emptively suspended classes on Friday across Poland, the majority in the Mazovian district, where the capital Warsaw is located. School directors sent messages announcing stepped-up security measures including extra school staff placed at entrances and voluntary backpack checks.

“There will be no compromise here. The safety of the youth is the most important thing,” Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said.

The government earlier said that it had so far found no evidence that an internet challenge promoting school attacks was ongoing. There is also no official confirmation that any of the attacks are linked.

articles.title: ABC News quietly republishes gutted version of story on Trump sons it had deleted without explanation
articles.summary: ABC News issued an editor's note admitting errors in its report on Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump's investments tied to Pentagon contracts.
articles.body: ABC News quietly republished a watered-down version of a previously deleted report scrutinizing the business dealings of President Donald Trump's oldest sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, on Friday evening. The original report, published earlier in the week, was removed following criticism of its accuracy. The original report, which remains accessible through the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, was published Wednesday afternoon under the headline, "Trump sons' investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election." ABC News removed the report less than 24 hours later without a public explanation at the time. However, the revised report reappeared on ABC News' website Friday with an editor's note, factual corrections and a new headline: "New shipyard announced amid earlier Democratic concerns about potential conflicts of interest." ABC NEWS DELETES ‘HIT PIECE’ ON TRUMP SONS' PENTAGON-LINKED INVESTMENTS WITHOUT EXPLANATION The article's byline was also changed to "ABC News." The editor's note acknowledged errors involving descriptions of company investments, government contracts and the chronology of events. "Editor’s Note: CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies," the statement read. "After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events." ABC News' decision to remove the report without an immediate public explanation drew criticism from media industry figures. ABC News' revisions followed public criticism from 1789 Capital spokesperson Alexa Henning, who disputed the original report's description of the firm's investments. Henning said "1789 Capital does not have a 'major stake' in Anduril" and challenged the article's characterization of the Trump brothers' involvement in other companies. "Here's a small lesson, that I also explained to ABC, the ‘reporter’ who is a complete idiot conflated raising funds with investment by 1789. Those are two separate actions," Henning wrote. 1789 Capital is the venture firm in which Trump Jr. serves as a partner. The initial report incorrectly attributed a $2.5 billion investment in Anduril to 1789 Capital. The revised article clarified that the figure represented the total funding Anduril raised last year. INSIDE TRUMP’S DEAL TO GIVE AMERICAN TAXPAYERS A MASSIVE STAKE IN NEW $6.6B SUBMARINE DEAL "1789 Capital — a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders — claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company," ABC News reported in the deleted story. The revised article also states that Trump Jr. does not sit on the three-person committee responsible for investment decisions, according to a spokesperson for 1789 Capital. The updated story states that 1789 Capital previously invested $50 million in defense contractor Anduril, which ABC valued at approximately $60 billion. The initial removal drew the attention of Trump Jr., who took to X to mock California Gov. Gavin Newsom after the story was taken down. "ABC deleted this article in less than 24 hours because it’s false. Sounds about as long as your presidential campaign would last," he wrote on X. Bill Ackman, founder and CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management, criticized ABC News on social media for removing the article without issuing a public correction at the time. articles.title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
articles.summary: Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".
articles.body:
Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".

The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.

The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.

"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.

The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.

The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.

It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".

The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.

Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.

Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure María Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.

Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway".

He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

articles.title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after failed execution
articles.summary: Pike's lawyers say she is "grateful" to the medical team who cared for her after she survived two lethal injections last month.
articles.body:
US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.

Pike, 50, has been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years and is continuing to receive medical care, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.

She survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition.

Pike regained consciousness earlier this week and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.

Her case is now in uncharted territory as she is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

Pike's lawyers said in their statement that she was "grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances".

It is unclear what medical care Pike is receiving now that she is back in prison but her lawyers previously said she faced a "long road to recovery".

The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.

I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's

At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he did not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again.

The judge ordered the state to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.

Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.

Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.

Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Tennessee Governor Bill Lee declined to block the execution.

Since it failed, Pike's lawyers have renewed their calls for her sentence to be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Pike lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital following her botched execution. Her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.

Pike eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyer Randy Spivey said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"

At a press conference on Wednesday, her lawyers said she was shackled to the bed and suffering from pneumonia and significant swelling on her arms, while also being unable to swallow.

"We don't know the toll all of this will take" Spivey said of her mental health, adding that Pike felt "angry and confused".

articles.title: Riyadh airport attacked again and evacuated as explosions rock the Saudi capital
articles.summary: The airport in the Saudi capital was attacked again on Saturday and evacuated, two regional officials said, two days after three Saudi citizens including a pilot were killed as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war.
articles.body: CAIRO — The airport in the Saudi Arabian capital, Riyadh, was attacked again on Saturday and evacuated, two regional officials said, two days after three Saudi citizens including a pilot were killed as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war. Flights to Riyadh diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said, almost four hours after the last flight landed at 2:05 p.m. Kuwait Airways said it was canceling flights because the airport had closed. Canada’s embassy advised citizens to avoid all travel to the airport, noting “ongoing military activity.” King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the earlier attacks, including one Wednesday that killed a Sudanese national. A resident said he heard explosions in Riyadh There was no immediate Houthi statement Saturday. The Saudi government-run Center for International Communication, which oversees foreign media in the kingdom, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. A Riyadh resident, Ahmed Sayed, told The Associated Press he heard at least two loud explosions that rocked the capital. The airport issued a terse alert telling passengers to check their flight status with airlines before heading to the airport. At least 225 flights at the airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces in an attempt to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. The rebels’ gains gave them better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that’s a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships. Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign ended that. Trump ‘not happy’ but no sign of new support The Saudis have sought support from the U.S. and other allies as its airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure have come under attack. Officials said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive. On Friday, as he left the White House, U.S. President Donald Trump was asked about the attacks on the Riyadh airport and told reporters, “It’s not good” and “I’m not happy.” But there has been no immediate sign of U.S. military support to respond to the attacks. The Saudi and Omani foreign ministers spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region, the kingdom said Saturday. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region. Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that “filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.” Flight disruptions are growing This week, the Houthis warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations. Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines have been among the airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for the next few days. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.” The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said. In Thursday’s attack, the Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.
