articles.title: California Democrat 'deeply disappointed' after Newsom vetoes reparations tax break
articles.summary: Assemblymember Tina McKinnor says she is "deeply disappointed" after Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed her California reparations tax exemption.
articles.body: A California lawmaker told Fox News Digital that she is "deeply disappointed" after Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed her bill that would have exempted future reparations payments from California's personal income tax. "I am deeply disappointed that Governor Newsom vetoed AB 2186. Reparations are not a gift or a government handout," Assemblymember Tina McKinnor, D-Inglewood, told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Reparations are meant to repair harm, not be partially taken back through taxation." Newsom vetoed the measure on Sept. 30 as he acted on a series of bills, including other reparations-related legislation. REPARATIONS ADVOCATES SLAM CASH COMPENSATION ‘HANDOUT’ LABEL, POINT TO PAST GOVERNMENT REMEDIES In his official veto message, Newsom acknowledged the bill's intent but cited fiscal uncertainty. "I thank the author for her continued work to redress the documented harms of slavery," Newsom wrote. "I was proud to sign into law last year legislation establishing the Bureau for Descendants of American Slavery, a first-in-the-nation law establishing a state agency that, among its key responsibilities, will advise on reparative justice programs for Black Americans. California's work on this important endeavor is just beginning." Newsom also cited uncertainty about the potential cost of the exemption. "Because the full scope of the proposed tax exclusion is unknown, fiscal caution is warranted," Newsom added. "The proposed exclusion for unspecified federal initiatives could be interpreted broadly, resulting in substantial fiscal uncertainty. Moreover, given the potentially significant General Fund implications, this measure should be considered as part of the annual budget process." CALIFORNIA COUNTY APPROVES REPARATIONS PLAN AS NEIGHBORING SCHOOL DISTRICT 'BLACK THRIVING' EFFORT STALLS Despite rejecting the tax exemption, Newsom signed another reparations-related measure into law. The first-in-the-nation law requires large companies doing business in California to scour historical records and publicly disclose slavery-era transactions, advancing the state's broader reparations push through a new corporate mandate. Assembly Bill 2599, authored by Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, D-Ladera Heights, applies to businesses with more than $100 million in annual worldwide gross receipts that existed—or have a predecessor entity that existed—on or before Dec. 31, 1964. Once funded by the Legislature, covered companies must submit sworn affidavits under penalty of perjury verifying searches for historical records involving the purchase or sale of enslaved people, their use as loan collateral, slave-related insurance policies, and other transactions. Covered companies will have until January 2029 to submit their first affidavits. CASH PAYMENTS ARE NOT 'RULED OUT' AS CALIFORNIA COUNTY OFFICIALS PUSH REPARATIONS FOR BLACK LOCALS McKinnor's measure, Assembly Bill 2186, was designed to exempt future reparations payments or benefits from California's personal income tax if qualifying state, local or federal reparations programs were established. Under the text of AB 2186, gross income would not have included "any reparations benefit or payment received by a taxpayer during the taxable year" for taxable years beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2028, and before Jan. 1, 2033. The bill defined a "reparations benefit or payment" as any monetary payment, grant, trust distribution, debt forgiveness, or other financial compensation provided through a qualifying reparations program. SOME BLACK NEW YORKERS DEMAND CASH PAYMENTS AS ONLY 'TRUE' FORM OF JUSTICE McKinnor emphasized that reparations payments are intended as compensation for generations of structural harm. "Reparations payments are compensation for generations of injustice, discrimination, and economic harm," McKinnor said. "California cannot claim to support reparative justice while taxing the very compensation intended to repair that harm. I respect the Governor's concerns about fiscal responsibility, but justice must also be a priority." "We cannot continue to study injustice, acknowledge the harm, and then hesitate when it is time to act," she added. "I remain committed to working with my colleagues and the new Governor to bring this legislation back in 2027. Justice delayed should not become justice denied." California was the first state in the nation to establish a formal task force to study the legacy of slavery and recommend potential restitution measures. However, concrete direct-cash payout initiatives at the state level have stalled over budget concerns and legal vulnerabilities. CHICAGO SUBURB EXPANDS CASH HANDOUTS AS RACE-BASED REPARATIONS PROGRAM FACES MAJOR LEGAL BATTLE Elsewhere in the country, localized reparations programs have moved forward with mixed success. Black residents in Evanston, Illinois, received $25,000 housing grants as part of a municipal program aimed at rectifying historic housing discrimination. Similar local and municipal initiative seeking to provide direct compensation or economic aid are being debated nationwide. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The broader future of state-funded reparations in California remains highly precarious. With Newsom vetoing multiple reparations proposals citing fiscal parameters and legal challenges, and with the upcoming gubernatorial race featuring candidates reluctant to endorse broad direct cash handouts, the state's path toward financial restitution remains uncertain. When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, Newsom's office said that "the veto message speaks for itself."

articles.body: Several people were wounded when King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, was struck by a missile on Saturday. The incident came two days after three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in what has become a new front in the expanding Iran war.According to an airport official, air traffic at Riyadh airport had been suspended. The official spoke on condition of anonymity, citing a lack of authorisation to speak to the media.King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times over the past week, since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. The Houthis claimed responsibility for earlier attacks, including one on Wednesday that killed a Sudanese national.Operations supended, travellers evacuatedFollowing the attack, operations at the airport were temporarily suspended and travellers were evacuated, while dozens of ambulances were seen rushing to the site. This came after the airport issued a brief alert urging passengers to check their flight status with airlines before heading there. According to flight-tracking platform Flightradar24, flights bound for Riyadh were being diverted to other destinations nearly four hours after the last flight landed at 2:05 pm local time.At least 225 flights at King Khalid International Airport had been cancelled over the preceding 24 hours, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.Airlines announce flight cancellationsKuwait Airways announced the cancellation of flights to and from the Saudi capital, citing the closure of Riyadh airport due to the “security situation”.Meanwhile, Air India Express and Air India have extended the suspension of flights to and from Riyadh amid the evolving situation in Saudi Arabia. Air India Express has cancelled its services until October 14, while Air India has extended the cancellations until October 15.Both airlines had earlier announced on Thursday that flights to and from Riyadh would remain cancelled until October 10.US, UK embassies issue alerts for their citizensThe US Embassy in Riyadh said it was aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport and urged American citizens in the Saudi capital to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.The UK Embassy also advised British nationals to stay away from the airport area following what it described as a “serious incident”.Two major Saudi conferences to proceed despite earlier attacksOrganisers of two major Saudi energy and investment conferences have confirmed that the events will proceed as scheduled this month despite earlier missile attacks on Riyadh airport.Amid widespread flight disruptions and travel advisories from the UK, France and Germany, organisers of the World Petroleum Congress, scheduled from Sunday to Thursday, assured delegates of their safety and suggested alternative routes to Riyadh, including a four-hour drive from Dammam.The Future Investment Initiative, launched by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as the kingdom's flagship investment conference a decade ago, would also proceed as planned from October 26-29.(With agency inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1971, two 23-year-olds began constructing a Hudson Valley castle with salvaged barn wood and scrap; 43 years later, it opened as a working bed-and-breakfast
articles.summary: Discover how Peter and Toni Ann Wing built Wing's Castle from salvaged materials, turning it into a unique home and bed-and-breakfast in the Hudson Valley over 47 years.
articles.body: When Peter and Toni Ann Wing began building their dream home in New York's Hudson Valley in 1971, they did not have a conventional house plan, a large construction budget or professional experience in building castles. What they had was a piece of family land, plenty of imagination and a willingness to use whatever materials they could find.According to the Hudson Valley Post, what began as a project the young couple expected to complete in about two years gradually became a 47-year undertaking. Over the following decades, the Wings built a stone-and-timber castle using reclaimed materials, including pieces from old barns and other structures around the Hudson Valley. The castle eventually became both their family home and a bed-and-breakfast.A castle that began as a homeThe property in Millbrook, Dutchess County, had been part of the Wing family farm. Peter had grown up nearby, and the site eventually became the setting for the castle he had promised to build for Toni. According to Architectural Digest, both were 23 when construction began. The original idea was much simpler than what eventually stood on the hill. Peter envisioned a barn-like structure with two silo-shaped sections. But once the basic form began to take shape, the towers looked more like parts of a medieval castle than an ordinary farm building. The couple decided to follow that unexpected direction rather than abandon it.Peter designed and constructed much of the castle. During the first three years of work, the couple actually lived on-site under a tarp while the castle gradually built up around them. Rather than purchasing all new materials, they found usable materials wherever they could. Materials from abandoned barns were used, while bricks, stones, windows, wood, and decorative pieces were utilised to build up the castle. Its uniqueness came from the mix of salvaged materials and the way they were shaped.From scrap materials to a medieval-looking structureUsing recycled materials was partly a necessity for the Wings, who did not have the funds to build a traditional custom castle from new materials. Being able to keep building while giving the structure its weathered look was an added benefit of using materials already available to them. Sources say the materials came from across the Hudson Valley region, including pieces from old barns.As time passed, the castle became more elaborate. Towers, stone walls, wooden beams, maze-like passageways and other unusual details made the place feel like a hand-built fantasy rather than an ordinary house. It also became part of the family’s routine: while Toni cared for the children, Peter kept building and working on his art and design.When the castle opened its doorsBy the 1980s, the strange structure had generated so much interest within the local community that the family began offering tours of it. However, Peter was not done yet. After finishing the initial structure, he began building another one to house guests. This other construction would take him another 22 years. Finally, the bed-and-breakfast facility would open its doors to visitors in 2014.Peter died in a car accident in 2014, shortly after the bed-and-breakfast opened. Toni and their son Charles were the custodians of the place after this. The castle continues to operate as a bed-and-breakfast where visitors can stay and take tours. Today, Wing's Castle stands as a reminder of one family's tenacity rather than a traditional historical building. The walls still contain remnants of the materials Peter and Toni gathered over the years, and the rooms still serve the purpose the project began with: making a home.You use AI every day. articles.title: Delhi protests: Mamata, Kejriwal and 7,000 protesters released; CJP leaders still in detention
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police have released over 7,000 protesters detained across the capital on Saturday, including four former chief ministers.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police have released over 7,000 protesters detained across the capital on Saturday, including four former chief ministers. However, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders will remain in custody as due legal process is followed, news agency ANI reported, citing police sources.The detentions came amid a massive security clampdown to prevent a planned protest at Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged vote theft.Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee, former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan, AAP convenor Arvind Kejriwal and former Tripura chief minister Manik Sarkar were among the opposition leaders detained while attempting to join the protest. All four have since been released.Mamata, who was released from detention in Delhi, referred to the President's remarks on the need for evidence to investigate the allegations. "But the President has said that 'We don't have any evidence; if we are to investigate, we need proof.' So we said, 'Fine, we will provide the proof.' This part is true," she said.Vijayan, who was released along with CPI(M) MP John Brittas and former Kerala minister KN Balagopal from Mandir Marg police station, criticised the Delhi Police's handling of the protesters."Delhi is witnessing the Modi government's ruthless crackdown on democracy. Protesters are being detained, while the government evades questions on electoral integrity. The behaviour of the Delhi Police today is completely unbecoming of a professional police force. But barricades and detentions cannot halt the march of democracy, and I am proud to have been a part of this protest against the denial of democracy and to defend our Constitution," he said.Kejriwal was released from Jaffarpur police station after his detention. He had earlier called on people across the country to reach Delhi and demand the chief election commissioner's resignation.CJP leaders remain in custodyCJP leaders Abhijit Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained by Delhi Police after their flight from Mumbai landed in the national capital. Police had told them they did not have permission to hold the protest at Jantar Mantar.Dipke accused the police of treating CJP leaders like criminals. In a pre-recorded video message released after his detention, he said the organisation's in-charge, Ajinkya Shinde, would lead the protest at Jantar Mantar. CJP maintained that the protest would continue nationwide, with or without its leaders.Police also informed Dipke about the death of his 85-year-old paternal grandmother, Savitribai Shankarrao Dipke, in Maharashtra's Hingoli district. She died at her home in Santuk Pimpri village around 11.30 am on Saturday after a prolonged illness. Family sources said police offered to facilitate his journey home on humanitarian grounds.YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, who lives abroad and had travelled to join the protest, was detained from his residence in Gurugram's Sector 56.Heavy security prevents protesters from reaching Jantar MantarThe authorities deployed more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel across Delhi to prevent protesters from gathering at Jantar Mantar. The designated protest site remained largely deserted throughout the day as barricades were placed across Lutyens' Delhi. Police also closed 45 metro stations and intensified checks at border points, railway stations, bus terminals, hotels and other sensitive locations.Police said more than 7,000 protesters were detained across the capital, including over 2,000 in the New Delhi area. Several opposition leaders and activists were among those detained, including CPI(M) general secretary MA Baby, veteran Left leader Brinda Karat, CPI(ML) Liberation general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya, activist Yogendra Yadav, lawyer Prashant Bhushan and All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Israeli combat medicine slashes IDF deaths after Oct 7, draws US military interest
articles.summary: IDF battlefield medicine cut combat mortality rates from 15% to 7.1%, with advances in casualty evacuation and trauma care now benefiting the U.S. Army.
articles.body: JERUSALEM — The growing number of Israeli army battlefield life-saving measures have emerged during the Iranian regime-backed multi-front war against the Jewish state that those new technologies are helping the U.S. too. Fox News Digital was briefed on the most current insights and data on Israel’s success rate in saving soldiers’ lives from a senior Israel Defense Forces (IDF) medical specialist in battlefield medicine. The grueling Israeli ground offensive against the U.S.-designated terrorist movement Hamas in the Gaza Strip, which started in Oct. 2023, following the Jihadi organization’s invasion of Israel on Oct. 7, introduced cutting-edge medical tactics to the battlefield. THE US-ISRAEL STRATEGIC ALLIANCE – PARTNERSHIP, NOT CHARITY Hamas brutally murdered over 1,200 people in southern Israel, including more than forty Americans, and kidnapped 251 people. An IDF spokesman laid out the new advances: "The IDF Medical Corps adapted its operational capabilities during the war, including casualty evacuation, innovative medical technologies and providing treatment under fire in a challenging terrain." The IDF medical specialist told Fox News Digital that during "the Second War in Lebanon [in 2006 against the Lebanese-based terrorist group Hezbollah] it took 15 to 20 minutes for advanced life support to reach a casualty. Now advanced life support can reach a casualty immediately or within 4 minutes." The placement of "medical personnel on the battlefield, including a doctor in every company, allows the IDF to make critical decisions early on during the care process," said the IDF medical specialist. The use of helicopters to deliver seriously wounded soldiers to medical facilities, as seen in video footage provided to Fox News Digital, plays a critical role in preventing death. The second advance is, according to the IDF medical specialist, "rapid evacuation," which means "We can evacuate casualties to Israeli hospitals rapidly." 5 OF AMERICA'S GREATEST MEDICAL BREAKTHROUGHS REVEALED AS THE NATION MARKS 250 YEARS There has been "an emphasis on the use of blood products since 2013 on stopping bleeding," said the IDF medical specialist. He added that the IDF is the first medical organization that "used plasma on the point of injury instead of salt and water." He noted the IDF implemented a sophisticated rapid-fire system for providing blood to injured soldiers. A telling example: Blood was placed on the back of first responders in coolers to stop bleeding and control the hemorrhaging. The method "saved significant numbers" of injured soldiers. An additional improvement in lifesaving first response medicine in the war zone involves an "advanced system of learning and the collection of data that transmits the data over technical networks so that every provider can see patient data." The IDF specialist said that "Every relevant medical officer on the chain can see the patient data. This system had very good results." The case mortality rate is the best index for quantifying care, said the IDF medical specialist. The results have been dramatic. According to IDF data, the mortality rate during the 2006 war against Hezbollah was 15% in contrast to 7.1% during 2023. The IDF medical specialist said Israel’s military medicine apparatus has relied on the bedrock 2012 U.S. study "Death on the battlefield (2001–2011): Implications for the future of combat casualty care," which covered American medical aid during the war in Iraq. Dr. Marc Siegel, senior medical analyst for Fox News, is also a clinical professor of medicine and a practicing internist at NYU Langone Medical Center, told Fox News Digital, "Battle field advances based on the latest technologies that have been developed in Israel, including surgical techniques as well as the latest burn treatment Nexobrid help not just today’s wounded but fuel medical and surgical advances around the world." Siegel's latest book "The Angels Among Us: How God's Messengers Play a Role in Healing," features a chapter involving a medical rescue during the Gaza war. The U.S. Army and the IDF have been cooperating in how to advance battlefield medicine for years. articles.title: Man dies after tiger attack at Yorkshire Wildlife Park
articles.summary: It was reported the man entered the tiger enclosure at the attraction near Doncaster, police say.
articles.body:
A man has died after being attacked by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, police have confirmed.

South Yorkshire Police said it had been called at 13:35 BST to reports of a man entering the tiger enclosure at the attraction near Doncaster. The tiger then attacked the man and he died at the scene, the force said.

His family had been informed and were being supported by officers, it added.

A park spokesperson said: "We are deeply saddened by today's tragic incident. Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies are with the family and loved ones of the person who has lost their life."

They added: "We are working closely with the police and relevant authorities and would ask that the privacy of those affected is respected at this extremely difficult time. The park will remain closed tomorrow."

Police said the tiger was uninjured, remained in the enclosure following the incident and there had been no wider risk to the public.

The park was evacuated and officers remain at the scene.

The force added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."

Earlier, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, was enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated.

She said she heard what sounded like "gunshots", and an air ambulance circled above.

Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure."

She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it was "very, very well organised".

Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with its Land of the Tigers area opening in 2011.

The purpose-built two-acre reserve is home to Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with around 500 left in the wild.

Photos of the enclosure on the park's website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.

articles.title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital and returned to Tennessee prison
articles.summary: Pike survived two doses of lethal-injection drugs on September 30, renewing scrutiny of capital punishment.
articles.body:
Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital and returned to a Tennessee women’s prison after surviving the US state’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said on Saturday.

The 50-year-old is back in the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she had been incarcerated for 30 years. She had been in hospital since September 30 when officials administered two doses of pentobarbital in an attempt to execute her.

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer.

Her lawyers said she was continuing to receive medical care in prison and that they would monitor her recovery. They also expressed gratitude to the first responders and medical team who treated her.

The failed execution has drawn attention to the US death penalty as a separate controversy unfolds over the military’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan. The former army psychiatrist was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. His execution is scheduled for December 3.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement on Thursday of the livestream drew criticism , even from some supporters of capital punishment. Vice President JD Vance questioned on Friday whether it would happen and said he would not watch. In a social media post, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called the proposal “beyond disgusting”.

Archbishop Paul S Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, also condemned the plan, calling it “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death”.

In Tennessee, however, Pike’s failed execution has not prompted Republican legislators to reconsider capital punishment. Instead, some have discussed alternative methods, including the electric chair and firing squads.

Support for the death penalty in the US has declined from its peak in the 1990s. Ten states have abolished capital punishment since Pike was sentenced in 1996, but executions continue nationwide.

Thirty people have been executed in the US this year, with eight more scheduled, mostly in Texas and Florida.

A Pew Research Center poll in July found that about two-thirds of US adults considered the death penalty morally justified for people convicted of murder. But roughly six in 10 said it did not deter crime, while about seven in 10 said there was some risk of an innocent person being executed.

articles.title: Drumcree dispute: Four key takeaways so far
articles.summary: BBC News NI's Political Editor Enda McClafferty assesses the fallout from the Drumcree dispute so far.
articles.body:
For a number of years in the 1990s, the Drumcree parade dispute was one of the biggest stories in Northern Ireland - and then, for 28 years, it fell out of the public eye.

However, that changed when the Parades Commission ruled that the march on Sunday 27 September could go ahead with restrictions in place.

That parade did not happen and, after a series of legal challenges and talks between residents and Orangemen, the secretary of state banned the procession .

On Saturday, a High Court judge said a legal appeal by Orangemen following the secretary of state's decision was not an emergency case and adjourned the hearing until Monday.

BBC News NI's Political Editor Enda McClafferty assesses the fallout so far.

Where does this leave the secretary of state?

As steep learning curves go, this one was off the scale.

Less than three months into the job, Sir Chris Bryant has had to make what will be the biggest decision of his time in Northern Ireland.

He will be forever remembered as the first secretary of state to ban what was a legal Orange parade.

But he says he was left with no option in the interest of peace.

The police had already ruled out forcing the parade through and when negotiations broke down, he had to step in.

The secretary of state had the power to act alone, but it was politically easier to have the cover of a police request.

Though making such a significant announcement late on Friday night was not ideal.

He clearly wants to move on with Westminster returning from recess on Monday and legacy legislation to be fast tracked through the Commons.

But the legacy of his Drumcree decision will follow him for some time and will likely scupper any hope he had of fostering good relations with unionists.

It could have been a moment of great jeopardy for power-sharing at Stormont.

The moment when the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) bowed to pressure and effectively collapsed the Executive.

But the party moved quickly to remove that threat within hours of the Orange parade being banned from the Garvaghy Road.

Party leader Gavin Robinson insisted they "will not sacrifice the stability of Northern Ireland and plunge it into further crisis".

To do so, he said, would allow "Sinn Féin an escape route from the spotlight and accountability".

For the DUP, pulling down the institutions was high risk with an election on the horizon.

History shows parties who walk away from Stormont pay a heavy price at the polls.

Especially before a budget is agreed to approve public sector pay rises thus avoiding strikes.

The DUP has opted instead to keep the focus on potential lawbreaking by Sinn Féin ministers.

It allows for more tough talking in the chamber even though the punishment if convicted will result in fines.

Though some in the DUP question if the institutions can be "sustainable" if First Minister Michelle O'Neill and her executive colleagues are found to have broken the law.

That will be a calculation for another time and much will depend on the proximity of polling day.

But the Drumcree dispute has delivered for Sinn Féin.

It provided the platform to supercharge its election campaign and helped deflect from questions around delivery at Stormont.

Though the court ruling clearing the way for the A5 has eased some pressure on the party.

But it delivered on its promise to residents to ensure no parade down the Garvaghy Road.

In truth any prosecutions they may face for standing with residents will be viewed by many within the party as a badge of honour.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) had five million reasons to bring the Drumcree dispute to an end.

That's how much the policing operation has cost for the past fortnight at a time when the police budget is already stretched.

A bill which would have been much higher had officers faced any violent disorder.

But the true cost for the PSNI may come in its relationship with the Orange Order and wider unionist community.

Allegations of two-tier policing have resurfaced but so far there have been no calls from unionist leaders for the chief constable to quit which is telling.

Forcing the parade through was never an option for the police.

Public safety risks aside, the potential to damage relations with nationalists was too great.

With the latest PSNI recruitment campaign being launched on Monday, the service couldn't afford to further alienate potential Catholic recruits.

It was a body set up to resolve parading disputes, not to restart them.

That has been the charge directed at the commission by many over the past fortnight.

Its determination, allowing an orange parade down the Garvaghy Road for the first time in 28 years, caught everybody by surprise, including those in the loyal order.

It also triggered a spat with the PSNI who tried to distance itself from the determination.

The commissioners are now the first to have their decision reversed by a secretary of state, although they will say conditions and the police advice had changed.

But there is no escaping the reality that public confidence in the body has been damaged.

Restoring that trust won't be easy, nor will finding replacements for the current commissioners when their term comes to an end.

articles.summary: US president Donald Trump on Saturday said Ukraine should get a new president, blaming Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to end the war with Russia, a day
articles.body: US president Donald Trump on Saturday said Ukraine should get a new president, blaming Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to end the war with Russia, a day after announcing a deal to ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies amid elevated US fuel prices.Speaking at the White House, Trump said, “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” adding that “for some reason (Zelenskyy) never does”.Trump also claimed that the war could have been prevented had he been US president in 2022. “There was no reason that that war with Ukraine and Russia started. articles.title: Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV describes capital punishment as an ‘attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person’ in post on X.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has declared that the death penalty is “inadmissible” while his home country, the United States, announces plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

Marking World Day Against the Death Penalty on Saturday, the pope reiterated the Catholic Church’s teaching on capital punishment, writing on X that it was “inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person”.

“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” his post said.

“Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption,” added the leader of the Catholic Church.

The American Pope’s comments come days after US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan on December 3 will be livestreamed.

Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009.

Pope Leo did not specifically refer to the planned execution, or last month’s botched execution attempt on Christa Pike , who survived two doses of the lethal injection in Tennessee.

But his post came hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, told Vatican News that the plan to livestream Hasan’s execution was “unacceptable”.

It was Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, in 2018 who first amended official Catholic teaching to declare capital punishment “inadmissible” in all circumstances.

Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of church teaching, said the church did not exclude recourse to capital punishment “if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against the unjust aggressor.”

The planned livestream of Hasan’s execution has sparked outrage across the US political divide. Republican representative Austin Scott said he supported executing Hassan but that “livestreaming executions is what Jihadists do. America is better than that.”

Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice”, but that public executions are “the kind of thing that Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?”

On Thursday, a Pentagon official confirmed the plans, but on Friday, Vice President JD Vance, who is a practising Catholic, expressed doubt on whether the livestream would be going ahead, telling reporters that if it is, “I’m not going to be watching it.”

articles.title: Expedition hopes to find aviator Amelia Earhart's plane on remote island
articles.summary: The team en route to the suspected crash site aim finally to solve the mystery of her 1937 disappearance.
articles.body:
A team of researchers are on their way to a remote island to inspect what they think could be the wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart's plane.

The group, from the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University, are expected to arrive at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean by Monday in the hopes of solving the mystery of her disappearance.

The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation on her fate.

The team are aiming to find what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020.

Purdue University said the object had since been confirmed to have been visible in aerial photography of the area dating back to 1938.

The researchers are currently roughly halfway through their journey to the remote atoll aboard the Marin Mainiku, a Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel.

They departed the capital of Kiribati on Wednesday to begin the 830-mile journey to Nikumaroro, which is also part of the multi-island country.

When they eventually arrive, they will have to navigate through a narrow gap created in the atoll's reef created by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.

"Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the ALI and the expedition lead, said.

Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.

From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.

But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.

Earhart's disappearance spawned numerous theories - from a simple crash due to fuel exhaustion to more elaborate claims of interference.

The official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems while the two struggled to find the island, and Earheart eventually crashed into the ocean when she ran out of fuel.

While this version of events is largely accepted, no physical evidence has ever been recovered.

One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.

Images of the so-called Taraia Object show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.

But some - including rival explorers - have expressed scepticism that this could be a plane, let alone Earhart's.

Ric Gillespie, who specialises in recovering historic aircraft wrecks, told news agency Reuters that the object looked like a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the nearby water.

"I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," he said.

The researchers en route to the island credit Gillespie with previously finding evidence of a human presence on the atoll in the 1930s and forensic analysis of skeletal remains found there in the 1940s they say lend credence to their theory.

But Gillespie suspects Earhart's plane had likely broken apart and its fragments carried into the depths of the Pacific long ago.

Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.

In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.

Similarly, an expedition in 2019, conducted by the marine archaeologist who discovered the Titanic wreck, to investigate a photograph of what might have been a landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

articles.title: A California house shaped like a flying saucer has hit the market for nearly $1.5 million; built in 1969, the 793-square-foot Futuro home is one of about 50 surviving examples of the space-age design
articles.summary: A house resembling a flying saucer has been listed for $1.495 million in California’s San Jacinto Mountains, offering a rare opportunity to own a piece of
articles.body: A house resembling a flying saucer has been listed for $1.495 million in California’s San Jacinto Mountains, offering a rare opportunity to own a piece of experimental architectural history. According to SFGATE and The Wall Street Journal, the property, known as the Donaldson Futuro, is located near Idyllwild and is among a small number of surviving homes designed to capture the optimism and futuristic imagination of the Space Age.Built in 1969, the 793-square-foot structure stands out for its bright exterior, circular form and distinctive raised design. Made from reinforced fiberglass-polyester plastic, the home weighs approximately 11,900 pounds and was conceived as a prefabricated dwelling that could be transported to different locations, even by helicopter. Designed by Finnish architect Matti Suuronen, the Futuro houses were an unconventional response to the era’s interest in new materials, mobility and futuristic living.A rare survivor of space-age architectureThe Donaldson Futuro is one of roughly 50 to 60 examples believed to remain from the original production of about 100 structures worldwide. Its unusual design has helped it stand apart from conventional residential architecture, while its historical significance has earned it a place on the National Register of Historic Places and recognition as a California historical landmark.The home’s journey to its current mountain setting was almost as unusual as its appearance. Originally located in San Diego, it was rescued after years of neglect and eventually transported to the Idyllwild area in 2004. Despite the original concept of helicopter-assisted mobility, the relocation required a carefully planned journey by flatbed truck through mountain roads, with the route presenting challenges because of the structure’s size and the limited clearance in some stretches.The preservation effort behind the homeThe property was saved and restored by preservation architect Milford Wayne Donaldson, who had been fascinated by space and futuristic design since childhood. He took on the project after learning that the neglected structure faced an uncertain future, seeing value in preserving an unusual example of mid-century architectural experimentation.Donaldson and his wife, Laurie, later restored the home while retaining its distinctive character. The interior reflects a 1960s aesthetic, with colourful finishes, laminate surfaces and shag carpeting. Original design elements, including built-in furniture and Formica laminate countertops, were preserved as part of the restoration, according to architectural preservation organisation Docomomo US. The project also involved navigating modern building and safety requirements while adapting them to the structure’s unconventional construction.The restoration received recognition from the California Preservation Foundation, while the home’s historic designation further established its importance beyond its novelty as a UFO-shaped residence. It is also noted as the first Futuro house in California approved for residential occupancy.A new chapter for the Donaldson FuturoDonaldson and his wife have continued to spend time at the property despite living near Sacramento. However, the architect’s declining health has prompted the decision to put the home on the market. The hope is that its next owner will appreciate its architectural and historical value and preserve the work that went into restoring it.Listed at $1.495 million, the property is more than an unusual home for sale. It represents a period when architects and designers imagined that houses could break free from traditional forms and embrace the possibilities of modern materials and technology. For its next owner, the Donaldson Futuro offers the chance to take on a rare piece of that vision, one that has survived decades of changing tastes and a challenging journey to its present mountain location.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Bill Maher mocks Mamdani for pivoting to Israel criticism in Oct. 7 tribute, calls it 'tone deaf'
articles.summary: Bill Maher blasted Zohran Mamdani's Oct. 7 anniversary statement on "Real Time," mocking the New York City mayor's pivot to criticizing Israel.
articles.body: Comedian Bill Maher took aim at New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his statement marking the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attack on Israel. Maher used Friday's episode of "Real Time" to criticize Mamdani's statement, in which the mayor called the day "profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers" and said the city grieves "alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss." Mamdani went on to condemn the ongoing defensive acts being carried out by Israel, writing, "The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children." ISRAEL AMB TORCHES MAMDANI OCT 7 POST: 'LIKE TURNING SEPTEMBER 11 INTO A DAY OF MOURNING FOR AL-QAEDA' The mayor continued, writing that "even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed," adding "many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them—all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes." Mamdani also wrote, "Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment." SCHUMER, JEFFRIES DODGE MAMDANI CONTROVERSY AS FELLOW NEW YORK DEM UNLOADS "To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity," the mayor said. Mamdani’s reaction to the anniversary did not go over well with Maher, who harshly criticized the mayor. BILL MAHER RIPS MACKLEMORE'S GAZA STANCE, SAYS CELEBRITY 'MORAL CONFUSION' IS FUELING ANTISEMITISM "Mayor Mamdani, not all that sympathetic to this stuff, but he did make some nice remarks about it," Maher said, referring to Mamdani’s statement. "But then he pivoted right to, ‘but Israel made them do it,’" Maher said, offering his interpretation of the mayor's remarks. ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTERS LABEL MAMDANI A 'TRAITOR,' ACCUSE HIM OF 'GENOCIDE' OUTSIDE OCT 7 VIGIL The comedian also mocked Mamdani's past career as a rapper, during which he performed under the stage names "Young Cardamom" and "Mr. Cardamom." "You know, he used to be a rapper. His rap name was ‘Tone Deaf,’" Maher quipped. Mamdani also faced criticism earlier this week after dining Wednesday at Ayat Hinds Hall, a Palestinian restaurant. The restaurant's sister location drew criticism in 2023 over menu language that critics described as antisemitic. The sister restaurant previously drew criticism after the Times of Israel reported that the front page of its menu featured the phrase "Down with the occupation" in English, Arabic and Hebrew. Owner Abdul Elenani previously said the language appeared on the menu before Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA' Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff, however, suggested that Maher's criticism could benefit Mamdani politically. "At first glance it could appear Mamdani missed the mark with his statement or is being ‘tone-deaf’ as Maher puts it — but I’d argue it was actually a page from the Trump playbook," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "Mamdani’s base was criticizing him for having NYPD protect Netanyahu, keeping on Commissioner Tisch, arresting protesters, not following through on his promise to disband the Strategic Response Group," Shroff continued. "And a tweet or statement that plays to what his base wants to hear, ruffles feathers, grabs headlines and earns some backlash is a way to try and placate his supporters and seem like a fighter on key campaign issues that he has actually backed away from. " Shroff went on to suggest Maher’s criticism of Mamdani is actually helping the mayor solidify his support from those who may have questioned his commitment to his campaign promises surrounding the Israel-Hamas conflict.
